items.title: Silicon Valley's elite is on edge awaiting results for California's Prop. 40 billionaire tax
items.summary: Californians are voting on a proposal that could send a one-time, huge tax bill to the state's billionaires. Lester Cohen/Getty Images It could be days or weeks before a final tally on California's Prop. 40 "billionaire wealth tax." Early results give the "No" vote a commanding lead among both Silicon Valley elites and rural Hispanic counties. It could bring in $100 billion to plug a coming Medicare hole — or lose billions in tax revenue. The morning after the midterms, there's still no answer on California's billionaire wealth tax — and the final results may not be in for days or even weeks. As of around 10:30 a.m. Eastern time Wednesday, 44.4% of California voters had thrown their support behind Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time "5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion." With about 60% of the vote in thus far, there's still plenty of time for the results to reverse, but the "No" vote has a commanding lead. More interesting is how support and opposition have played out across the Golden State. The socially-progressive urban strongholds of Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Alameda County (home to Berkeley and Oakland) are favoring the measure with slim majorities. Meanwhile, many of the poorer and majority-Hispanic agricultural communities in California's Central Valley and desert regions have come out against the wealth tax by double-digit margins. Rural California has an unusual bedfellow in wealthy Silicon Valley. Counties representing Palo Alto, Cupertino, and the hilly Peninsula cities that house much of the Bay Area's venture capital and post-exit founder class have come out firmly against the tax so far. Other solid-blue Western states look set to pass narrower progressive tax measures. Washington state, which hasn't voted in favor of an income tax since 1932, went firmly against repealing a "millionaires tax" passed by the state legislature earlier this year. In Colorado, an amendment that would replace the state's flat income tax with a progressive scheme is leading by a thin margin. Amendment 87 would raise taxes on the wealthy and businesses while cutting them for most Coloradans. California's vote is the culmination of a showdown that's been shaking up Silicon Valley executives for months. Google cofounder Sergey Brin , former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Affirm CEO Max Levchin, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Kleiner Perkins Chairman John Doerr, and angel investor Chris Larsen have collectively poured millions into an opposition campaign . Brin himself has donated more than $100 million to the "No" team, per Cal Matters. State campaign-finance filings show committees opposing Prop. 40 had reported about $130 million in contributions through October 22, versus about $33 million for its supporters. Meanwhile, other tech executives are preparing, just in case they have to pay up. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg weighed moving out of the state. In October, the company created a new class of shares that would give Zuckerberg $20 billion in "immediate liquidity" if the vote passes — potentially allowing him to pay the tax without giving up some of his voting power. "I've got to tell you, I have not even thought about it once," Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, said during a January spot on Bloomberg TV. "We chose to live in Silicon Valley, and whatever taxes they would like to apply, so be it. I'm perfectly fine with it." The vote has also split some regular political alliances. Progressive Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders has backed the billionaire tax, while California's Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, opposes the measure. There are multiple paths to "No" If a majority of voters fill in the "Yes" bubble on Prop 40, roughly 200 people who were California residents on January 1, 2026, could face the one-time tax. That vote has two lurking trap doors — propositions 41 and 42 could ruin the "Yes" team's finale. As of Wednesday morning, the "No" side on Prop. 41 was winning with 52.5% of the vote, while Prop. 42 was up with 54.3% in favor. Both countermeasures were designed to undercut Prop. 40 by imposing new auditor reviews and prohibiting taxes on certain assets. If either measure receives more yes votes than Prop. 40, the billionaire tax could be stopped from taking effect, even if a majority of Californians vote for it. What California's billionaires could owe In broad terms, the measure would tax billionaires based on more than their salary. Taxable wealth would include ownership stakes in businesses, securities, investment accounts, art, collectibles, and intellectual property, among other assets. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts would generally be excluded. If the billionaire tax passes, it'll be due in 2027 — though taxpayers could spread out their payments across five years at a higher cost. Supporters say the measure could raise tens of billions of dollars over several years. items.summary_html:
Californians are voting on a proposal that could send a one-time, huge tax bill to the state's billionaires.

Lester Cohen/Getty Images

  • It could be days or weeks before a final tally on California's Prop. 40 "billionaire wealth tax."
  • Early results give the "No" vote a commanding lead among both Silicon Valley elites and rural Hispanic counties.
  • It could bring in $100 billion to plug a coming Medicare hole — or lose billions in tax revenue.

The morning after the midterms, there's still no answer on California's billionaire wealth tax — and the final results may not be in for days or even weeks.

As of around 10:30 a.m. Eastern time Wednesday, 44.4% of California voters had thrown their support behind Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time "5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion."

With about 60% of the vote in thus far, there's still plenty of time for the results to reverse, but the "No" vote has a commanding lead.

More interesting is how support and opposition have played out across the Golden State. The socially-progressive urban strongholds of Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Alameda County (home to Berkeley and Oakland) are favoring the measure with slim majorities.

Meanwhile, many of the poorer and majority-Hispanic agricultural communities in California's Central Valley and desert regions have come out against the wealth tax by double-digit margins.

Rural California has an unusual bedfellow in wealthy Silicon Valley. Counties representing Palo Alto, Cupertino, and the hilly Peninsula cities that house much of the Bay Area's venture capital and post-exit founder class have come out firmly against the tax so far.

Other solid-blue Western states look set to pass narrower progressive tax measures.

Washington state, which hasn't voted in favor of an income tax since 1932, went firmly against repealing a "millionaires tax" passed by the state legislature earlier this year.

In Colorado, an amendment that would replace the state's flat income tax with a progressive scheme is leading by a thin margin. Amendment 87 would raise taxes on the wealthy and businesses while cutting them for most Coloradans.

California's vote is the culmination of a showdown that's been shaking up Silicon Valley executives for months.

Google cofounder Sergey Brin, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Affirm CEO Max Levchin, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Kleiner Perkins Chairman John Doerr, and angel investor Chris Larsen have collectively poured millions into an opposition campaign. Brin himself has donated more than $100 million to the "No" team, per Cal Matters.

State campaign-finance filings show committees opposing Prop. 40 had reported about $130 million in contributions through October 22, versus about $33 million for its supporters.

Meanwhile, other tech executives are preparing, just in case they have to pay up.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg weighed moving out of the state. In October, the company created a new class of shares that would give Zuckerberg $20 billion in "immediate liquidity" if the vote passes — potentially allowing him to pay the tax without giving up some of his voting power.

"I've got to tell you, I have not even thought about it once," Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, said during a January spot on Bloomberg TV. "We chose to live in Silicon Valley, and whatever taxes they would like to apply, so be it. I'm perfectly fine with it."

The vote has also split some regular political alliances. Progressive Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders has backed the billionaire tax, while California's Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, opposes the measure.

There are multiple paths to "No"

If a majority of voters fill in the "Yes" bubble on Prop 40, roughly 200 people who were California residents on January 1, 2026, could face the one-time tax.

That vote has two lurking trap doors — propositions 41 and 42 could ruin the "Yes" team's finale. As of Wednesday morning, the "No" side on Prop. 41 was winning with 52.5% of the vote, while Prop. 42 was up with 54.3% in favor.

Both countermeasures were designed to undercut Prop. 40 by imposing new auditor reviews and prohibiting taxes on certain assets.

If either measure receives more yes votes than Prop. 40, the billionaire tax could be stopped from taking effect, even if a majority of Californians vote for it.

What California's billionaires could owe

In broad terms, the measure would tax billionaires based on more than their salary.

Taxable wealth would include ownership stakes in businesses, securities, investment accounts, art, collectibles, and intellectual property, among other assets. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts would generally be excluded.

If the billionaire tax passes, it'll be due in 2027 — though taxpayers could spread out their payments across five years at a higher cost.

Supporters say the measure could raise tens of billions of dollars over several years. A majority of the proceeds would go toward healthcare, with the remainder allocated to education, food assistance, and the operation of the tax program. The campaign has pitched the measure as a way to help backfill looming federal cuts to Medi-Cal.

Overall, Prop. 40 backers have said the tax event would raise over $100 billion for the state.

A National Bureau of Economic Research working paper from Stanford economists, published in October, warned that the results could be much less rosy. The initial tax event could bring in around $30 billion before prompting high-earning executives to leave the state, the paper said. That could lose California $38.9 billion over time, the paper warned.

items.title: Business winners and losers from the 2026 midterm elections
items.summary: The midterm elections sent millions of Americans to the polls. Here's what we learned from the early results. Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images The midterms ended on Tuesday, sending a fresh batch of lawmakers to Washington and state houses. Americans also decided on ballot measures. Those decisions could determine future business projects. AI companies and the stock market have been some of the biggest losers of the night. There's a new set of power brokers in government, and it's creating winners and losers when it comes to companies, industries, and policies. In the 2026 US midterms , which ended on Tuesday, voters handed the Democratic Party control of the House and the Senate. Voters also cast ballots in governor races, state legislative races, and on ballot measures. Those results will help determine which projects receive funding, which companies face new regulations, and which policies are blocked over the next two years. From affordability candidates to mega-donor Elon Musk, here are the winners and losers in the 2026 midterm elections. Winner: Candidates running on affordability Hakeem Jeffries made affordability a key part of his campaign. Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images The Democratic Party will control Congress, with majorities in the House and Senate. The result is a surprisingly strong showing for Democrats, many of whom put affordability at the center of their campaigns. The cost of living frequently came up as a key issue for voters , with Americans shelling out more at the gas pump than a year ago as the war in Iran has pushed up prices. "We will fight hard to lower the high cost of housing and groceries and gas," said Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who will likely become Speaker of the House in January, in a Tuesday night speech. While many Republicans also ran on affordability policies, President Donald Trump acknowledged in a call with Fox News that midterm voters weren't willing to pay more for gas . "I don't think it's the war, I think it's the gas prices," Trump said. Loser: Elon Musk Musk was the biggest disclosed individual donor in the midterms race. Brandon Bell/Getty Images Musk spent more than $400 million trying to keep Republicans in power. It wasn't enough. He put the cash behind Republican-aligned groups this cycle, making him the biggest disclosed individual donor in the midterms. His biggest bet was on Ken Paxton's Senate campaign in Texas, where Musk-backed groups spent about $212 million. Democratic lawmaker James Talarico defeated Paxton anyway, helping Democrats take the Senate — and undercutting Musk's effort to preserve Republican control in the state he has made home to Tesla and SpaceX. Musk also used X, his social media platform, to tout Republican candidates, especially in Texas. "The fate of Texas and America is at stake," he wrote on X while endorsing the state's Republican Senate candidate, Ken Paxton. Meanwhile, he called James Talarico, Paxton's opponent, "a creep." Texas is also a personal political battleground for Musk. Tesla moved its corporate headquarters to Austin in 2021, while Tesla and SpaceX both reincorporated in Texas in 2024. SpaceX is now based at Starbase, Texas . He said he moved the companies to the Lone Star State for more favorable tax, land acquisition, and corporate legal policies. Loser: AI companies Data center buildout was a key mandate in the midterm polls. Kaylee Greenlee/Bloomberg via Getty Images AI companies are likely to face a tougher political environment. Democrats are expected to use their new control of Congress to scrutinize the costs of the AI race: the power and water consumed by data centers, rising household electricity bills, and whether tech companies are keeping enough of their promises about local jobs. That could mean more investigations and scrutiny of companies such as Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, and the firms building the data centers that support them. But the results won't necessarily mean a crackdown on AI. The president, who is pro-AI development and pro-AI infrastructure, can veto major legislation. There is also bipartisan agreement on AI regarding national security, competition with China, and economic growth. Winner: The stock market US stock futures fell after the Democratic sweep became clear on early Wednesday. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/Getty Images Initially, investors were not fans of the "blunami" that has swept election results. US stock futures fell after the Democratic sweep became clear, with S&P 500 futures down about 1% and Nasdaq 100 futures down nearly 2% in early trading. The dollar also weakened sharply against most major currencies as investors braced following a strong Democratic showing. AI-linked stocks were among the hardest hit, as investors weighed the prospect that Democratic control could mean tougher oversight of Big Tech and its data center spending. The trend reversed after markets opened. The S&P 500 was up about 1.5% in morning trading, while the Nasdaq index was up about 2.1%. SpaceX and Tesla , both of which have AI businesses, were each down about 2.5% in morning trading, although they pared some of their steeper premarket declines. Loser: People counting on $5,000 checks from Trump Those waiting for Trump's proposed $5,000 "dividend" might have to keep waiting. Trump made the promise conditional on Republicans keeping control of the House and Senate, an outcome voters have rejected. Even if Trump revived the idea, he would need Congress to authorize and fund it since the president cannot unilaterally spend more than $1 trillion on nationwide checks. Democratic control makes this even less likely. Read the original article on Business Insider

His biggest bet was on Ken Paxton's Senate campaign in Texas, where Musk-backed groups spent about $212 million. Democratic lawmaker James Talarico defeated Paxton anyway, helping Democrats take the Senate — and undercutting Musk's effort to preserve Republican control in the state he has made home to Tesla and SpaceX.

Musk also used X, his social media platform, to tout Republican candidates, especially in Texas.

"The fate of Texas and America is at stake," he wrote on X while endorsing the state's Republican Senate candidate, Ken Paxton. Meanwhile, he called James Talarico, Paxton's opponent, "a creep."

Texas is also a personal political battleground for Musk.

Tesla moved its corporate headquarters to Austin in 2021, while Tesla and SpaceX both reincorporated in Texas in 2024. SpaceX is now based at Starbase, Texas. He said he moved the companies to the Lone Star State for more favorable tax, land acquisition, and corporate legal policies.

Loser: AI companiesData center buildout was a key mandate in the midterm polls.

Kaylee Greenlee/Bloomberg via Getty Images

AI companies are likely to face a tougher political environment.

Democrats are expected to use their new control of Congress to scrutinize the costs of the AI race: the power and water consumed by data centers, rising household electricity bills, and whether tech companies are keeping enough of their promises about local jobs. That could mean more investigations and scrutiny of companies such as Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, and the firms building the data centers that support them.

But the results won't necessarily mean a crackdown on AI. The president, who is pro-AI development and pro-AI infrastructure, can veto major legislation. There is also bipartisan agreement on AI regarding national security, competition with China, and economic growth.

Winner: The stock marketUS stock futures fell after the Democratic sweep became clear on early Wednesday.

Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Initially, investors were not fans of the "blunami" that has swept election results.

US stock futures fell after the Democratic sweep became clear, with S&P 500 futures down about 1% and Nasdaq 100 futures down nearly 2% in early trading. The dollar also weakened sharply against most major currencies as investors braced following a strong Democratic showing.

AI-linked stocks were among the hardest hit, as investors weighed the prospect that Democratic control could mean tougher oversight of Big Tech and its data center spending.

The trend reversed after markets opened. The S&P 500 was up about 1.5% in morning trading, while the Nasdaq index was up about 2.1%.

SpaceX and Tesla, both of which have AI businesses, were each down about 2.5% in morning trading, although they pared some of their steeper premarket declines.

Loser: People counting on $5,000 checks from Trump

Those waiting for Trump's proposed $5,000 "dividend" might have to keep waiting.

Trump made the promise conditional on Republicans keeping control of the House and Senate, an outcome voters have rejected.

Even if Trump revived the idea, he would need Congress to authorize and fund it since the president cannot unilaterally spend more than $1 trillion on nationwide checks. Democratic control makes this even less likely.

items.title: Uber needs drivers. It wants to throw your money at the problem
items.summary: Uber is shifting spending from rider discounts to incentives for drivers to work more. Sebastian Gollnow/picture alliance via Getty Images Uber is trying to lure drivers to work more on its app. From the US to India, the company is spending more on driver incentives, CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said. It's a challenge that Uber has not faced since the end of the pandemic. Uber needs drivers, which means some riders will be shelling out more cash. In the US and abroad, the ride-hailing and delivery service is spending money to coax drivers to take more trips and deliveries, CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said on the company's third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday. Rider prices might even increase as a result. That's a change from last year, when Uber was spending more to attract more customers to use its app, Khosrowshahi said. "This year, we're taking down rider incentives, and we're using those dollars to fund driver incentives," he said on the call. The shift in spending "does mean sometimes higher prices for riders, which is something that we watch out for," Khosrowshahi added. Uber has not faced a driver shortage this bad in years. The last time that the company talked about increasing spending on extra payments for drivers was in 2021, when it faced a driver shortfall after the pandemic forced many gig workers to stay off the road. Since then, many drivers have faced lower pay after accounting for their expenses. Riders, meanwhile, have contended with higher per-mile fares and longer wait times on Uber , according to a study published in September. Uber has offered some US drivers hundreds in incentive payments this fall ahead of the busy holiday season, Business Insider reported last month. The problem is broader than the US, though, executives said on Wednesday's call. Uber is also investing in attracting more delivery workers to its Uber Eats business, Khosrowshahi said. And both drivers and customers in emerging markets such as Brazil and India are being squeezed by higher fuel prices, CFO Balaji Krishnamurthy said. Fuel prices have spiked in the months since the US and Israel started a war with Iran. Uber is spending on incentives for drivers in those markets, too, Khosrowshahi said. AI is deciding exactly how and where Uber spends its incentive money, Khosrowshahi said. Uber's algorithms are trained on "billions of trips" and make decisions "that humans just can't," he said. "If you have a dollar, what is the maximum predicted return for that dollar?" Khosrowshahi said. "The algorithms are making these choices," he added. Do you have a story idea about Uber? items.title: Data centers got a slap in the face at the ballot box. These key votes show how.
items.summary: Gina Hinojosa became Texas' first Democratic governor in over 30 years. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images Data centers got a big fat "no" from the American people on Tuesday. Dozens of local elections included referendums on their construction. Democrats broke through in Texas, which is home to hundreds of data centers. Americans don't want data centers in their backyards. That's one of the clearest messages sent at the ballot box during Tuesday's midterm elections . NBC News' exit poll found that 76% of voters would oppose the construction of a new data center in their community, and 56% said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress. As well as governors and senators who voiced opposition to data centers winning, ballots included referendums on their construction. Goldman Sachs economists said Democratic wins at the state and local levels will likely lead to "short-term data center moratoria, potentially affecting about 45% of planned US data center capacity expansion." More than 30 direct votes against data centers passed Dozens of cities and small towns held referendums in which data centers were directly on the ballot. As of 8 a.m. ET, voters had approved 33 ballot measures restricting data centers, versus one allowing them, according to an analysis by Redbud Consulting. Most of these votes were in Ohio, home to a key data center for OpenAI's $500 billion Stargate project . One measure stands out as being linked to a specific project. EdgeConneX wanted permits from the town of Ashville to build two data centers on a 195-acre property. However, 82% of its 1,800 voters rejected a resolution to proceed with the development of data centers and an associated natural gas facility. Americans look set to vote overwhelmingly against data centers in many of the referendums. For example, in Alhambra, a city in Los Angeles County, a measure to ban data centers is also on track to be approved by 82% of voters. A blue swing in data center hot spot Texas James Talarico celebrates after winning the Senate race in Texas. RONALDO SCHEMIDT / AFP via Getty Images Texas was one of the clearest examples of the " blue tsunami ," in which Democrats exceeded expectations. It's also a major location for data centers, including Stargate's flagship site plus two others under development. The gubernatorial race was a particular upset, where Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate, beat the incumbent Greg Abbott. She will be the state's first Democratic governor since 1995. Her campaign included a promise to immediately pause data-center development in the state. With 96% of the votes counted, Hinojosa had a 7-point lead, per the Associated Press — an 18-point swing from the last gubernatorial election in 2022. James Talarico, the Democratic senator-elect, has argued that data centers are contributing to the cost of living, including by increasing utility bills. He also wants to create an "AI dividend" for people to share in AI companies' profits. 'Data Center Alley' swings further to the Democrats Sen. Mark Warner retained his seat with huge swings compared to the presidential election. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Virginia has the most data centers of any state. The majority of those are concentrated in the north, giving the region the nickname " Data Center Alley ." Loudoun County has some 250 operational data centers, and over 100 more planned. While many analysts expected the state to stay blue, Democratic Sen. Mark Warner extended his majority. Statewide, there was a 17-point swing compared to the 2024 presidential election. With 97% of votes counted in Loudoun County, Warner received 69% of the vote. That's a 21-point swing compared to 2024, and an 11-point swing from the state's last Senate election in 2020. A blue swing in data center hot spot Texas James Talarico celebrates after winning the Senate race in Texas.

RONALDO SCHEMIDT / AFP via Getty Images

Texas was one of the clearest examples of the "blue tsunami," in which Democrats exceeded expectations. It's also a major location for data centers, including Stargate's flagship site plus two others under development.

The gubernatorial race was a particular upset, where Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate, beat the incumbent Greg Abbott. She will be the state's first Democratic governor since 1995.

Her campaign included a promise to immediately pause data-center development in the state.

With 96% of the votes counted, Hinojosa had a 7-point lead, per the Associated Press — an 18-point swing from the last gubernatorial election in 2022.

James Talarico, the Democratic senator-elect, has argued that data centers are contributing to the cost of living, including by increasing utility bills. He also wants to create an "AI dividend" for people to share in AI companies' profits.

'Data Center Alley' swings further to the DemocratsSen. Mark Warner retained his seat with huge swings compared to the presidential election.

Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

Virginia has the most data centers of any state. The majority of those are concentrated in the north, giving the region the nickname "Data Center Alley."

Loudoun County has some 250 operational data centers, and over 100 more planned.

While many analysts expected the state to stay blue, Democratic Sen. Mark Warner extended his majority.

Statewide, there was a 17-point swing compared to the 2024 presidential election.

With 97% of votes counted in Loudoun County, Warner received 69% of the vote. That's a 21-point swing compared to 2024, and an 11-point swing from the state's last Senate election in 2020.

items.title: AI and blockchain are coming to African farms: 4 things must happen for farmers to benefit
items.summary: The use of digital agriculture is expanding across Africa. Tools like artificial intelligence (AI), sensors and blockchain are helping farmers receive information about weather, pests, markets and farm management. AI can analyse images and other farm data to detect problems or support decisions. Digital traceability systems can record where food comes from and what happens to it along the supply chain. These technologies offer considerable opportunities, particularly in horticulture. Fruits and vegetables are highly perishable, so a decision made at the wrong time can result in substantial losses. But does better technology on its own produce better farming? We are researchers specialising in horticultural science, post-harvest technology, agricultural engineering, crop quality and sustainable food systems. In a recently published paper, we investigated this question. We reviewed studies published between 2005 and 2025 to examine how AI and blockchain are used in farming, their potential benefits and the barriers farmers face. We found that many existing approaches focus heavily on what the technology can do, such as tracking produce, automating processes and verifying digital records. They pay less attention to the people expected to use these systems, the conditions under which they operate and the rules governing how agricultural information is collected and shared. What’s missing are clear rules about who controls farm data, how farmers benefit and how digital systems can meet the needs of smallholder farmers. Based on these insights, we propose combining AI’s ability to predict problems with blockchain’s ability to protect records. Together, they could help farmers make better decisions and track their produce. The aim is to support more sustainable horticultural production and distribution, ensure that smallholder farmers can participate and benefit, and establish clear rules for how information is managed and decisions are made. We identified four issues that need much more attention. 1. Smart technology needs good data As agricultural decisions become increasingly data-driven, checking the quality of the data becomes crucial. Blockchain is a shared digital record book. It allows approved users to store and check information. Farmers can use it to record information about their produce and share it with buyers. One attraction of blockchain is that records stored on it can be difficult to alter. In agriculture, this can strengthen traceability. For example, a blockchain can record where a crop was grown, when it was harvested and how it reached the buyer. Approved users can then check these records. But blockchain has an important limitation. It can protect information after it has been recorded. It cannot guarantee that the original information was correct. A sensor measures things such as temperature, moisture or light. But what happens if it gives an incorrect reading? A farm worker might also enter the wrong information. Putting that information on a blockchain does not correct it. It may simply create a secure record of inaccurate information. An AI model trained on poor-quality data could produce an unreliable recommendation. An AI model is a computer system that learns from data to identify patterns, make predictions or suggest actions. Our research identifies this as an important weakness, particularly in agricultural blockchain systems. The reliability of the final record still depends on the quality of the information entering the system. 2. Farmers need decisions, not simply more information Our review found that digital tools can produce large amounts of information. But that information is not always useful to farmers. Imagine that a system correctly predicts that a crop is under stress, but the farmer receives the warning too late to do something about it.
items.summary_html:
The use of digital agriculture is expanding across Africa. Tools like artificial intelligence (AI), sensors and blockchain are helping farmers receive information about weather, pests, markets and farm management. AI can analyse images and other farm data to detect problems or support decisions. Digital traceability systems can record where food comes from and what happens to it along the supply chain.

These technologies offer considerable opportunities, particularly in horticulture. Fruits and vegetables are highly perishable, so a decision made at the wrong time can result in substantial losses.

But does better technology on its own produce better farming?

We are researchers specialising in horticultural science, post-harvest technology, agricultural engineering, crop quality and sustainable food systems. In a recently published paper, we investigated this question.

We reviewed studies published between 2005 and 2025 to examine how AI and blockchain are used in farming, their potential benefits and the barriers farmers face. We found that many existing approaches focus heavily on what the technology can do, such as tracking produce, automating processes and verifying digital records. They pay less attention to the people expected to use these systems, the conditions under which they operate and the rules governing how agricultural information is collected and shared.

What’s missing are clear rules about who controls farm data, how farmers benefit and how digital systems can meet the needs of smallholder farmers.

Based on these insights, we propose combining AI’s ability to predict problems with blockchain’s ability to protect records. Together, they could help farmers make better decisions and track their produce. The aim is to support more sustainable horticultural production and distribution, ensure that smallholder farmers can participate and benefit, and establish clear rules for how information is managed and decisions are made.

We identified four issues that need much more attention.

1. Smart technology needs good data

As agricultural decisions become increasingly data-driven, checking the quality of the data becomes crucial.

Blockchain is a shared digital record book. It allows approved users to store and check information. Farmers can use it to record information about their produce and share it with buyers. One attraction of blockchain is that records stored on it can be difficult to alter. In agriculture, this can strengthen traceability. For example, a blockchain can record where a crop was grown, when it was harvested and how it reached the buyer. Approved users can then check these records.

But blockchain has an important limitation. It can protect information after it has been recorded. It cannot guarantee that the original information was correct.

A sensor measures things such as temperature, moisture or light. But what happens if it gives an incorrect reading? A farm worker might also enter the wrong information.

Putting that information on a blockchain does not correct it. It may simply create a secure record of inaccurate information. An AI model trained on poor-quality data could produce an unreliable recommendation. An AI model is a computer system that learns from data to identify patterns, make predictions or suggest actions.

Our research identifies this as an important weakness, particularly in agricultural blockchain systems. The reliability of the final record still depends on the quality of the information entering the system.

2. Farmers need decisions, not simply more information

Our review found that digital tools can produce large amounts of information. But that information is not always useful to farmers. Imagine that a system correctly predicts that a crop is under stress, but the farmer receives the warning too late to do something about it.

Read more: Kenya’s farmers have lots of digital tools to help boost productivity – how they can be made more effective

African smallholder farmers also operate under very different conditions. Some have smartphones and reliable internet access. Others work where connectivity is weak, mobile data is expensive or digital skills are limited. These are among the barriers to digital agriculture identified by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization.

Therefore, technology cannot simply be designed elsewhere and handed to farmers for adoption. Farmers and other users should be involved in its design. Some services may need to work offline. Others may require local languages, simple text messages or voice-based communication.

3. Who owns the farmer’s data?

Digital agriculture is also creating a valuable agricultural resource: data. A farm can generate information about soils, crop performance, pest outbreaks, fertiliser use, water, yields, weather and market transactions. Combining information from thousands of farms can make it more useful. The data could help train AI models, develop agricultural products, assess risk or support lending and insurance decisions.

That raises an important question: who controls and benefits from the data? Agricultural data governance already raises concerns about ownership, privacy, access and the bargaining power of farmers dealing with digital service providers. Farmers generate valuable data but have limited power over how it’s subsequently used.

If farmers provide the information that makes a digital system valuable but have little control over what happens to it, digital agriculture could reproduce existing inequalities rather than remove them.

4. Farmers need a reason to adopt the technology

A technology may improve traceability, generate sophisticated reports or produce impressive dashboards. But farmers still have to invest time learning the system and may have to pay for devices, connectivity or services. There must be a clear benefit. Economic value needs to be part of the design from the beginning.

Read more: Digital solutions are boosting agriculture in Kenya, but it’s time to scale up. Here’s how

That benefit could be reducing crop or post-harvest losses, lowering input costs, improving yields, obtaining better prices or gaining access to new markets. This matters particularly for smallholders operating with limited capital. Cost, inadequate digital skills and weak infrastructure can all restrict adoption. If exporters, retailers, technology companies or regulators receive most of the benefits while farmers carry much of the cost of supplying the data, sustained adoption becomes difficult.

What needs to change

These four issues don’t mean Africa should turn away from AI, blockchain or other useful agricultural technologies.

Our research proposes a framework in which data collection, AI, blockchain-based verification, automated decision support and feedback work together.

There is another layer surrounding all of them: governance. This means setting clear rules. Who can access farm data? Who checks decisions made by AI? Who takes responsibility when something goes wrong? How are farmers protected? For example, community-governed data arrangements are one possible response.

Farmers could have a meaningful role in deciding how their data are collected, shared and reused. Farmer groups could help. By working together, smallholders may have more say over how their data are used.

Before expanding digital agriculture, governments, technology developers and agribusinesses should ask whether the information is reliable, whether farmers can act on the recommendations, who controls the data and whether the technology delivers measurable benefits.

Africa does not need more technology for its own sake. Farmers need tools that work in their conditions and help them make better decisions. The next breakthrough may not be another app, algorithm or blockchain. It may be making the technologies we already have genuinely useful to the people growing the food.

items.title: AIhub coffee corner: Are humanoids the future of embodied AI?
items.summary: The AIhub coffee corner captures the musings of AI experts over a short conversation. This month we ask whether humanoids are the future of robotics. How has the technology evolved recently, and what can we expect in the years to come? Joining the conversation this time are: Joydeep Biswas (University of Texas at Austin), Sanmay Das (Virginia Tech), Rina Dechter (University of California, Irvine), Ioannis Erripis (AIhub), Sabine Hauert (University of Bristol), Ella Scallan (AIhub), and Marija Slavkovik (University of Bergen). Lucy Smith: There have been huge advancements in humanoid robots over the past couple of years. Today’s topic is particularly timely, as RoboCup 2026 recently took place. I thought it would be interesting to start with an overview of recent developments at RoboCup. Joydeep Biswas: This all started snowballing a couple of years ago, and we suddenly started to see this huge inflection on the capabilities. New humanoid robots were showing up at RoboCup that didn’t fall down as much. Suddenly we were able to deploy robots without humans following them around. I want to highlight that this is not just one key technical innovation, it required the confluence of a wide number of things: much better hardware, significant advances in algorithms, and advances in how we train and learn. Once upon a time, humanoid robots required classical control. However, most modern humanoid robots are using learned controllers for walking. So the rise of doing sim-to-real, like training these models in simulation and transferring them to the real world, are new algorithmic innovations. This year we had 55 humanoid robot soccer teams at the international competition, which is a lot for an international competition. We had a demo game of 11 vs 11 humanoid robots . Every year we have the RoboCup trustees play against the robots to see where we’re at. It used to be trivial. I won’t say it was hard this year, but I will say it’s getting less easy for the trustees as the years go by. RoboCup has recognized that we are at the inflection point, and at the trustees level we’ve been thinking about how to restructure our competitions to focus on these big advances coming up. We’ve simplified our soccer leagues significantly – in 2028, there will only be humanoid league soccer. Once upon a time, we couldn’t have a fully integrated humanoid robot capable of doing everything. Even though it’s not perfect today, we have the ability to integrate control, perception etc. We feel that from the scientific perspective, it is worth exploring having everything integrated into one robot form. Sabine Hauert: I started out excited about robotics because of RoboCup. I was in Manuela Veloso’s team doing the aibo (robot dogs) league. And that got me excited about robots working together. And then from there, they went on to the Nao robots and then to the humanoids. I guess this is a way to shake things up and to get it to the next level. Generally, I think the humanoid shift has been fascinating. And looking at ICRA and IROS , just the sheer shift in what’s on that exhibit floor over the years is really quite drastic. It used to be all drones and then it was all robot dogs and now it’s all hands and humanoids. There are also some of the more industrial robots that have been there for a while. But that shift is very striking because you walk around and there’s just so many of them. And at the robot parade you just see all these humanoid form factors and it’s very exciting from the hardware perspective. In addition there have been beautiful advances in the control to make that hardware and shape form work. I’m very excited for other robots, actually, not necessarily humanoids, because some of that technology can be transferred. I don’t know that we need humanoids for everything. I’m still very much in the category of people that think we need task-specific robots so that we can build them for the things that they’re meant to do. Maybe we get a general form factor not through having a human form, but by having lots of different robots with different form factors that work together, giving you the same capabilities as a human, but through multiplication rather than putting everything in one agent. But humanoids are part of the ecosystem, and I think they’re boosting the field, and so there’s a lot to gain from that. Ella Scallan: Are humanoids the most effective shape to get tasks done? Joydeep: No! The argument has been that everyday environments are designed for the human factor. So if you could have a working robot which has a humanoid factor, they could be a drop-in replacement and be able to use the tools and the environments which humans can. There is one big presupposition there: that we have functioning humanoid robots. As of today, that is absolutely not the case. In fact, if you want to have something work well today, there are very few cases where you could argue that the humanoid robot is the best solution. I think being a researcher in this area, it’s great to actually think a little bit about how we get to that eventual goal. Humanoids are rarely the correct solution for an application. Simple tasks, which are what we would call kinematic planning (for example, they are position-based – you want to pick up a block and put it somewhere else), are better with a wheeled robot, because the base is stable, and much easier with simpler planners, which have fewer degrees of freedom. You add a humanoid, suddenly the complexity increases. Now you’re not just worrying about position, you’re worrying about position and forces and velocities and accelerations which has much higher dimensions for planning. And it’s just not very easy to do. There are many more reasons too, that’s just one example. Marija Slavkovik: Can I give a historical anecdote here in response to that? A humanoid shape is not necessarily the best thing. Douglas Bader was a pilot in the Royal Air Force in the Second World War. He was considered to be a better pilot because he didn’t have legs, which he lost in an accident. And because he didn’t have legs, he was able to better handle high acceleration. There are some pretty horrible examples of children being used because their smaller bodies were better suited to the task, like kid jockeys on camels, children in mines, or in weaving. Of course, these are all examples of people, but their bodies are not what you think about when you say humanoid robot. Sanmay Das: I mean, it’s an interesting set of questions. I was wandering around one of these big conventions recently, and it was all about AI and robotics and very government tech/dev tech-focused. But one of the things they had that people were really interested in was this robot barista. You could ask it to make a coffee and it was going around doing things with the arms, but it wasn’t producing particularly good coffee from what I could tell. And I was thinking I have a semi-automatic espresso machine that I press a button on that does a really good job of making good coffee. I don’t see why we need this extremely complicated thing. But at the same time, people like it, right? How much of this is that people are more comfortable engaging with robots in this form? I think that one of the main things that we need to be careful about is anthropomorphization. I think for robotics, especially as they become more and more capable, this is really going to become a question. People will anthropomorphize these humanoid robots in ways that they will not your Roombas and your robot dogs and so on, and do we want that? And I think that that’s going to be an interesting question to think about. Ella: Even creating humanoid robots is an act of anthropromorphization.They aren’t the most effective shape for the task, so we’re sacrificing some function for form. Marija: Speaking of what we want, I’ve seen videos of robots that roll into a bathroom and clean it. They use the same brush for the toilet and the sink, but that’s a separate problem. My question is: how realistic are these? Because they’re just promotional videos: “invest now, and in one year, these are going to be real” . I even see some folding laundry, which is the holy grail, right? Robotics wise, are we there yet? Joydeep: I think you bring up an excellent point, which is truth in advertising. We are definitely seeing a lot of new capabilities that we didn’t have before, but we have to be honest about what they are and are not capable of. For many actors, it is in their best interests to promote the best of their platforms and hide the worst just because of the financial incentives. If you think a little bit about what went into setting up the demo, how many takes did it actually take you to do it? How over engineered was it for that very specific scenario? It worked with a particular brush, what if I gave it a slightly different brush? What if the light was turned off and it was on? And I can tell you the answer here is that none of these solutions are really robust. They’re definitely not general purpose. The best advancements are definitely over-optimized to very specific scenarios. Also the ways in which they’re being trained are just not scalable for doing the wider broad set of things that we want to do. So I think as a community, we need to demand and require truth in advertising. And the downside of this huge influx of companies in the space is that the incentives for scientific advancement are not necessarily well aligned with the advancement of companies today. Sabine: I think there’s a sense that people think it’s been done because they’ve seen it in a video, when a lot of it is either remote controlled or very fine-tuned for the scenarios that they’ve been designed for, as Joydeep mentions. There isn’t a “get your humanoid out-of-the-box and have it doing something useful in an environment it’s never seen before” because the data’s not there, it’s not been trained there. Joydeep: Yes. Even for a wheeled robot, we don’t have that capability. Rina Dechter: Thinking about one use case, robotics for social interaction with humans, for example if you wanted healthcare assistance or similar, psychologically it might give a better impression if you were assisted by a humanoid than a box. It may make a difference to people. But in other cases I agree, the best form for the robot depends on the tasks. Joydeep: I 100% agree. I think also it’s the challenge of the latest capabilities of our current research algorithms, because behind the capabilities that we’re seeing today are things like reinforcement learning and learning from demonstration. This is great for non-human interactive stuff like manipulating objects, but it doesn’t really scale well to human interaction. Marija: Well, we now have people being paid to do manual movements that are supposed to be somehow used for training afterwards. The AIhub coffee corner captures the musings of AI experts over a short conversation. This month we ask whether humanoids are the future of robotics. How has the technology evolved recently, and what can we expect in the years to come? Joining the conversation this time are: Joydeep Biswas (University of Texas at Austin), Sanmay Das (Virginia Tech), Rina Dechter (University of California, Irvine), Ioannis Erripis (AIhub), Sabine Hauert (University of Bristol), Ella Scallan (AIhub), and Marija Slavkovik (University of Bergen).

Lucy Smith: There have been huge advancements in humanoid robots over the past couple of years. Today’s topic is particularly timely, as RoboCup 2026 recently took place. I thought it would be interesting to start with an overview of recent developments at RoboCup.

Joydeep Biswas: This all started snowballing a couple of years ago, and we suddenly started to see this huge inflection on the capabilities. New humanoid robots were showing up at RoboCup that didn’t fall down as much. Suddenly we were able to deploy robots without humans following them around. I want to highlight that this is not just one key technical innovation, it required the confluence of a wide number of things: much better hardware, significant advances in algorithms, and advances in how we train and learn. Once upon a time, humanoid robots required classical control. However, most modern humanoid robots are using learned controllers for walking. So the rise of doing sim-to-real, like training these models in simulation and transferring them to the real world, are new algorithmic innovations.

This year we had 55 humanoid robot soccer teams at the international competition, which is a lot for an international competition. We had a demo game of 11 vs 11 humanoid robots. Every year we have the RoboCup trustees play against the robots to see where we’re at. It used to be trivial. I won’t say it was hard this year, but I will say it’s getting less easy for the trustees as the years go by.

RoboCup has recognized that we are at the inflection point, and at the trustees level we’ve been thinking about how to restructure our competitions to focus on these big advances coming up. We’ve simplified our soccer leagues significantly – in 2028, there will only be humanoid league soccer. Once upon a time, we couldn’t have a fully integrated humanoid robot capable of doing everything. Even though it’s not perfect today, we have the ability to integrate control, perception etc. We feel that from the scientific perspective, it is worth exploring having everything integrated into one robot form.

Sabine Hauert: I started out excited about robotics because of RoboCup. I was in Manuela Veloso’s team doing the aibo (robot dogs) league. And that got me excited about robots working together. And then from there, they went on to the Nao robots and then to the humanoids. I guess this is a way to shake things up and to get it to the next level.

Generally, I think the humanoid shift has been fascinating. And looking at ICRA and IROS, just the sheer shift in what’s on that exhibit floor over the years is really quite drastic. It used to be all drones and then it was all robot dogs and now it’s all hands and humanoids. There are also some of the more industrial robots that have been there for a while. But that shift is very striking because you walk around and there’s just so many of them. And at the robot parade you just see all these humanoid form factors and it’s very exciting from the hardware perspective. In addition there have been beautiful advances in the control to make that hardware and shape form work. I’m very excited for other robots, actually, not necessarily humanoids, because some of that technology can be transferred.

I don’t know that we need humanoids for everything. I’m still very much in the category of people that think we need task-specific robots so that we can build them for the things that they’re meant to do. Maybe we get a general form factor not through having a human form, but by having lots of different robots with different form factors that work together, giving you the same capabilities as a human, but through multiplication rather than putting everything in one agent. But humanoids are part of the ecosystem, and I think they’re boosting the field, and so there’s a lot to gain from that.

Ella Scallan: Are humanoids the most effective shape to get tasks done?

Joydeep: No! The argument has been that everyday environments are designed for the human factor. So if you could have a working robot which has a humanoid factor, they could be a drop-in replacement and be able to use the tools and the environments which humans can. There is one big presupposition there: that we have functioning humanoid robots. As of today, that is absolutely not the case. In fact, if you want to have something work well today, there are very few cases where you could argue that the humanoid robot is the best solution. I think being a researcher in this area, it’s great to actually think a little bit about how we get to that eventual goal. Humanoids are rarely the correct solution for an application. Simple tasks, which are what we would call kinematic planning (for example, they are position-based – you want to pick up a block and put it somewhere else), are better with a wheeled robot, because the base is stable, and much easier with simpler planners, which have fewer degrees of freedom. You add a humanoid, suddenly the complexity increases. Now you’re not just worrying about position, you’re worrying about position and forces and velocities and accelerations which has much higher dimensions for planning. And it’s just not very easy to do. There are many more reasons too, that’s just one example.

Marija Slavkovik: Can I give a historical anecdote here in response to that? A humanoid shape is not necessarily the best thing. Douglas Bader was a pilot in the Royal Air Force in the Second World War. He was considered to be a better pilot because he didn’t have legs, which he lost in an accident. And because he didn’t have legs, he was able to better handle high acceleration. There are some pretty horrible examples of children being used because their smaller bodies were better suited to the task, like kid jockeys on camels, children in mines, or in weaving. Of course, these are all examples of people, but their bodies are not what you think about when you say humanoid robot.

You could ask it to make a coffee and it was going around doing things with the arms, but it wasn’t producing particularly good coffee from what I could tell. And I was thinking I have a semi-automatic espresso machine that I press a button on that does a really good job of making good coffee. I don’t see why we need this extremely complicated thing. But at the same time, people like it, right? How much of this is that people are more comfortable engaging with robots in this form? I think that one of the main things that we need to be careful about is anthropomorphization. I think for robotics, especially as they become more and more capable, this is really going to become a question. People will anthropomorphize these humanoid robots in ways that they will not your Roombas and your robot dogs and so on, and do we want that? And I think that that’s going to be an interesting question to think about.

Ella: Even creating humanoid robots is an act of anthropromorphization.They aren’t the most effective shape for the task, so we’re sacrificing some function for form.

Sabine: The other thing I heard is that people are calling everything humanoids, so the word has taken over. It’s got a lot of excitement, it’s helping to raise funds. And then you’ll have a wheeled humanoid, or a humanoid with six arms, for example. And there will all be forms of humanoids. So it’ll go full circle back to the different form factors.

Marija: If you think about it, a computer playing chess does little for solving general AI tasks. But it acted as a catalyst to attract attention, funding and resources so that they can be used to actually develop deep learning and so on. So maybe it works out in the end. You create this magic for people to believe in and invest in, and something else comes out of it. Although I’m not going to say I’m advocating this, it’s definitely borderline fraud sometimes, these videos of depicted abilities. It’s just easier to sell, right?

That was the trick, Sabine, that whenever somebody asks you when we are going to see useful or capable humanoids, you can ask them what they mean by useful or capable. Because then you turn around the question. People understand that we already have very many useful and capable things.

Sabine: Yeah, so they were asking when the breakthrough was going to be. I say the breakthrough is when we see all those robots that work in everyday environments, not necessarily humanoid, and all the things we’re pushing research-wise out in the world. And I think that’s the breakthrough.

Joydeep: I think even before ChatGPT was released December 2022, and folks who were playing with these large language models, GPT 2, 3, etc, we were seeing capabilities which were very hard to do beforehand. What really made it break through in the public consciousness was having a public-facing website – that was an inflection point. I doubt that for the robotic space we’re going to see a similar inflection point where suddenly we’re able to see generational new capabilities. I think we’re probably going to see slow adoption of robots in limited capabilities and specific scenarios, increasingly more and more and more. It’s just going to be a very slow adoption. We’re not going to suddenly have a robot capable of doing it all.

Marija: If any of you see a robot that folds laundry or irons laundry, wake me up in the middle of the night. To me, that’s the breakthrough point. If I see one of them, I don’t care how much it costs.

Joydeep: Well, again, the question is, under what conditions? If you are okay with a few hours to fold your laundry and specific kinds of laundry.

Marija: It can take as much time as it wants, let’s make it one week maximum. But no caveats. You have to take it out of the dryer and fold it in a neat stack, unspecified laundry. I mean, think about it. Would you care how long it takes as long as it’s done? How long does it take me, the lazy human to do it? Three days it’s going to live in the dryer until I get to it.

Joydeep: Yeah, so the challenges here are robustness. So you said it should not matter what the laundry is, and you want a certain degree of accuracy. You don’t want that every fifth attempt, it makes a catastrophic failure, and then you have to go rescue the robot. Now, not only do you have to do your laundry on your own, you also have to rescue the robot. I think as humans we have very high expectations for autonomy, which we don’t explicitly mention, which is fine, but I think that’s the challenge. In research papers, we say that an 80% success rate is phenomenal. No, 80% success rate as a product is awful. It’s a failure. Or even 99%, it’s still not good enough.

Ioannis Erripis: I have two small questions. Firstly, I’ve seen recently at least three companies that are advertising household humanoid robots. What do you think about those?

Sabine: The remote controlled ones.

Joydeep: Yeah, there’s certainly not anything which can do all household tasks autonomously. They’re actually using you for data collection.

Sabine: There’s a company in San Francisco that will pay you to do your household cleaning, because they collect data from your house.

Ioannis: My second question is more maybe superficial. What do you think about the design of most of the humanoid robots? And let me rephrase this a bit more specifically. One of my favourite robots was maybe Honda’s ASIMO, which looked like an astronaut toy. If you see behind the glass, it is smiling and has a very cute face. It’s a robot that you would easily give as a gift to your child, for example. But almost all humanoid robots are very menacing. They almost look like a villain from a movie. And actually, at the same time, they aspire to be adopted by consumers. What do you think about this? To me, it looks like a very unorthodox approach.

Joydeep: I think you’re absolutely right, but there are companies which are trying to build humanoid robots which are human approachable. Fauna Robotics is one of them. They are very much leaning into exactly what you’re saying.

Ioannis: I guess that’s an exception.

Joydeep: I agree it’s an exception, and I think partly that is because the capabilities that we’re really missing today are these fine-grained motor skills. People are trying to think about whether we can just build a form and understand how we can solve these fine-grained motor skills, and then we’ll talk about the interaction. But you’re absolutely right that we should think about them jointly.

items.title: Why AI is Eating Google Search’s Ad Revenue While Boosting Meta’s
items.summary: The third quarter of 2026 offered an interesting insight into how AI is creating two different outcomes for the world’s largest digital advertising businesses. While Meta is using AI to improve ad targeting, recommendations, and campaign performance, Google faces a new challenge: monetising users who increasingly interact with its AI-powered search. In Q3, Meta reported advertising revenue of $63.06 billion, up 26% year-on-year. Google’s Search and other advertising revenue grew 12% to $63.35 billion, down from 17% in the previous quarter and 19% in the first quarter. Surprisingly, Search accounted for less than 50% of Google revenue for the first time. Is Google in Trouble? Chatbots such as ChatGPT , Anthropic’s Claude, and Meta’s new Muse assistant are becoming alternatives to traditional search. People ask these tools questions and get direct answers instead of clicking blue links on Google results pages. Fewer clicks mean fewer ad views and less revenue for Google. Google’s own AI features are also part of the shift. AI Overviews and AI Mode give users summaries and conversational answers. “The real shift is towards zero-click search. One AI conversation now does the work of five or six searches, and the user never lands on a results page where the ad lives. That is where the keyword model is exposed,” Viren Inaniyan, Co-founder and CEO of Tru Commerce, tells AIM. Google said AI Mode queries are, on average, three times longer than normal searches. Yet these AI experiences currently earn less money per query than traditional search. “Google has indicated that AI Mode currently monetises at a lower rate than traditional search. Part of this challenge is that most Google searches already end without a click, a pattern often called zero-click. AI Mode adds another dimension to this, as customers can now get more complete answers without needing to visit another page,” says Jacob Joseph, VP – Data Science, CleverTap Philipp Schindler, Google’s Chief Business Officer, said AI Mode’s lower monetisation contributed to the slowdown in Search revenue growth. The challenge is that AI-generated answers can satisfy users without requiring them to visit multiple websites or click through several search results. This could reduce opportunities for traditional sponsored links, particularly if users increasingly complete their research within AI interfaces. Schindler attributed the sequential slowdown in Search revenue growth primarily to foreign exchange movements, which he described as the single largest factor. Vertical-specific spending trends also weighed on growth, with retail advertisers in APAC affected by the EU’s elimination of its de minimis exemption, while media and entertainment spending normalised after a FIFA World Cup-driven surge in Q2. For Google, the question is how to introduce advertising into AI Mode and AI Overviews without affecting answer quality or the user experience. Inaniyan says fewer clicks do not mean lost revenue. “Many of these queries are new research that never happened before. The question is whether Google earns more or less from the full journey, not per query,” he notes. Meta Turns AI into Advertising Revenue Meta’s approach is different. Rather than replacing its core discovery and social media experiences with conversational search, the company is using AI to improve how users discover content and how advertisers reach them. Its recommendation systems determine what users see across Facebook and Instagram feeds, Reels and other surfaces. Better recommendations can increase engagement, create more ad opportunities, and improve the likelihood that users will respond. “Meta does not need users to change how they buy. People keep scrolling and discovering. AI quietly improves what they see and which ad reaches them,” says Inaniyan. Meta reported that advertising impressions across its family of applications increased 10% year-on-year in Q3 2026. The average price per advertisement rose 14%, while Family daily active people (DAP) increased 3% year-on-year to 3.64 billion. The company attributed the rise in ad prices partly to improved ad performance. Meta is investing in AI models that can understand user preferences and match advertisements more accurately. During its earnings call, the company discussed its Generative Recommender, which uses large language models to reason across advertising content and user preferences to predict which advertisement is most relevant to an individual. In the third quarter, Meta deployed this approach on Facebook Feed, resulting in a nearly 2% increase in conversions across targeted segments. “Meta’s advantage comes from the combination of behavioural signals, candidate selection, conversion prediction and creative variation. Generating thousands of creative variants has limited value unless the delivery system can identify which variant works for which person and context,” says Kartik Sharma, Founder, Rankinllm.ai Meta also expanded its GEM model for advertising rankings to additional surfaces. This resulted in a 1.7% increase in conversions for off-site conversion campaigns and a 9.6% increase in app advertising conversions. Meta is also using generative AI to help advertisers create content. Nearly 10 million advertisers used at least one of its generative AI creative tools during the quarter. Adoption of its video-generation features rose 25% sequentially. The company is also developing its AI Business Assistant to help businesses manage campaigns and identify opportunities to improve performance. Meta said advertisers using its recommendations generated almost 5% more conversions at the same cost per conversion and increased their advertising investment by 9% compared with similar advertisers who did not use the assistant. Can Google Reinvent itself? Google is already working on new advertising formats. On October 28, the company announced it would expand ads in AI Mode to international markets, including India, Australia, Canada, Malaysia, New Zealand, Pakistan, the Philippines, Singapore, Kenya, and Nigeria. The company is also introducing multi-turn advertisements in AI Mode in the US, allowing ads to appear during follow-up queries. Google said internal research found that users consider AI Mode ads relevant. The formats are intended to give advertisers opportunities to reach consumers while they research products and compare options through conversational search. “Ads need to fit naturally into multi-turn conversations and be clearly labelled to maintain customer trust. This could mean moving beyond conventional keyword-based placements towards contextual recommendations, sponsored product comparisons and formats that become relevant as a conversation progresses,” says Joseph. He adds that Google would need more comparison and purchase decisions to happen within AI Mode to monetise it effectively, as early-stage queries generate limited advertising opportunities. “Advertisers will also need to measure campaigns against actual outcomes, placing greater emphasis on qualified leads, conversions and purchases rather than relying primarily on clicks and impressions.” Inaniyan argues that revenue per query is the wrong metric for Google to focus on. He says the company needs to monetise decisions users make within a conversation, not the clicks that take them to other websites. “That means ads become offers. Users should be able to compare, get a quote, book or buy directly within the answer. Product data becomes the ad unit. Catalogues, prices, availability and delivery information must be accurate, or the offer will not match what the user is looking for,” he says. Similarly, Sharma says Google needs to rethink how it measures and monetises advertising in AI-powered search. “Revenue per completed commercial task may ultimately be more informative than revenue per query,” he notes. “Advertising needs to respond to the user’s intent at different stages of a conversation. Someone researching a product category, comparing alternatives or requesting a quotation has different commercial intent at each stage. An expensive click is worthless if the recommended product does not meet the user's requirements,” Sharma says. He adds that advertising formats will also need to evolve beyond traditional sponsored links. Product comparisons, live inventory, quotations and booking options could become more relevant in AI-generated answers. Sharma says advertisers will want to see whether these new ad formats bring in additional customers and generate better conversions before committing more budget. He also highlights that serving AI-powered search experiences could increase costs. “Multi-turn reasoning, information retrieval and tool calls can increase infrastructure costs, making efficient model routing and caching important for profitability.” What’s Next for the advertising industry? Joseph believes advertising budgets will increasingly be distributed across feeds, AI search, chatbots and autonomous agents based on their ability to deliver measurable business outcomes. He expects this redistribution to take place over the next three to five years rather than an immediate shift away from established platforms. “Google and Meta already have significant advertiser relationships, data and monetisation infrastructure, but they will need to adapt as discovery increasingly happens through conversational AI and autonomous agents,” he notes.
