items.title: 84% See AI Productivity Gains, but Only 10% Allow Agent Autonomy: TCS Study
items.summary: Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) found that 84% of executives across enterprises identified productivity improvements as the leading benefit of AI investments. However, only 10% of enterprises allow AI agents to execute decisions without human approval across multiple business functions. Only 9% of executives reported that their organisations had AI agents that could securely orchestrate workflows across enterprise applications. Security, risk and governance emerged as the leading considerations when organisations decide where and how to deploy AI systems. These factors ranked ahead of cost, speed and ease of deployment. Amit Kapur, Chief AI and Services Transformation Officer at TCS, said, “What seems to be holding organisations back – and rightly so – are concerns around security, governance, and resilience.” He added, “Deploying AI responsibly, with the right guardrails and enterprise controls, will be the big focus in the next stage of this journey.” As agents gain access to enterprise systems, observability becomes important for monitoring their actions and decisions. The study also found that 90% of respondents considered model independence an important factor in AI investment decisions. However, only 7% reported having organisation-wide continuity plans to switch AI providers. About 34% of respondents identified AI sovereignty requirements, including control over data location, model choice, and regulatory compliance, as a high or very high organisational risk. In Europe, the figure rose to 43%. Separately, legacy systems, fragmented data and integration gaps are emerging as obstacles to scaling AI deployments. A recent assessment of Indian enterprises highlighted infrastructure challenges in moving AI workloads into production, as organisations assess whether their existing infrastructure can support AI at scale. AI economics remain unsettled. Thirty-nine percent of enterprises said they were still assessing whether their AI initiatives generated sufficient value relative to token and compute costs. Fidelity International has introduced use-case-level token budgets and an internal AI gateway to monitor expenditure and restrict access. Its approach to managing AI costs and model access offers an example of how organisations are addressing these concerns. Meanwhile, 44% of respondents said important business knowledge remained embedded in employees' expertise or fragmented documentation, potentially limiting AI systems' access to enterprise context. Another 46% reported deploying open-source AI for selected use cases. The proportion of leaders who said it was too early to determine AI's effect on jobs rose from 4% in 2024 to 19% in 2026. North America showed particular strength across several enterprise AI foundations, with 15% of respondents treating AI as a strategic enterprise capability. The UK and Ireland reported comparatively higher levels of continuity planning and governance integration. The study, titled Intelligence that is Real, surveyed 1,333 senior business and technology leaders across 25 countries and 12 industries. Their organisations had annual revenues ranging from $500 million to more than $20 billion.

items.title: Tech layoffs: A 2026 timeline
items.summary: Among a range of factors leading to a wave of tech sector layoffs in 2026 is the rapid rise of artificial intelligence and automation. Companies are reconfiguring their workforces to leverage AI for increased efficiency and reduced operating costs. This realignment and reduction is implemented even by companies reporting strong financial performance. But it’s not just AI leading to workforce cuts. Complementing this technological shift are ongoing economic uncertainty, inflation, and higher interest rates, compounded by a chip shortage and rising energy costs. This mix is driving companies to cut costs and streamline operations for increased efficiency. According to data compiled by Layoffs.fyi , an online tracker that keep tabs on job losses in the technology sector, 139,004 tech employees have been laid off at 345 companies so far in 2026, compared to the 122,606 layoffs it reported in 2025. Here is a list — to be updated regularly — of some of the most prominent technology layoffs the industry has experienced recently. Notable tech layoffs in 2026 Canva Oracle (again) Monday.com Microsoft Meta Cisco Cloudflare Oracle Atlassian Salesforce Amazon Ericsson Nov. 3, 2026: Canva lays off 22% of staff as it flattens org chart and consolidates teams Canva didn’t explicitly blame AI for a massive round of lay-offs that will see 1,271 staff, over one-fifth of its workforce, lose their jobs, but CEO Melanie Perkins did give a nod to how “ New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use ” in an open letter outlining the changes. To simplify and speed up decision-making around product development, she wrote, Canva is folding its product, growth, and platform teams into a single product organization, removing layers of middle management, reducing specialization by giving staff broader responsibilities, and requiring staff to show up more often at its office in Sydney, which will become the hub for product development. Sept. 15, 2026: Oracle forecasts 33% increase in restructuring costs as new round of layoffs hits Oracle began a new round of layoffs this week, sending early-morning termination emails to staff for the second time in six months. Oracle has made no public statement confirming the latest round of job cuts, but in a regulatory filing days earlier the company said it had set aside a further $700 million for restructuring charges, bringing the total charges this year to roughly $2.8 billion. July 22, 2026: Monday.com cuts 20% of its workforce to restructure for the AI era The company says the decision to cut 620 jobs isn’t about margins, but about creating a flatter organization built around AI agents, autonomous teams, and deeper customer engagement. July 6, 2026: Microsoft cuts 4,800 jobs, primarily in sales and Xbox teams As the company trims thousands of jobs , it’s also investing in embedded engineering teams and AI infrastructure. The layoffs come several weeks after the company offered 8,750 US employees voluntary retirement buyouts . June 5, 2026: Tech industry cut 38,242 jobs in May, worst since 2024 AI was blamed for 40% of the job cuts in May , up from 7% in January, according to research by employment placement company Challenger, Gray & Christmas. May 20, 2026: Meta cuts 8,000 jobs, around 10% of workforce The cuts are expected to expected to hit Meta’s engineering and product teams the hardest, arriving as Meta pivots toward AI to boost efficiency across its organization, according to Yahoo Tech . May 13, 2026: Cisco to cut nearly 4,000 jobs despite strong growth in AI, enterprise networking Despite reporting positive financial news — including record third-quarter revenue of $15.8 billion, a 12% year-over-year increase — Cisco said it will eliminate almost 4,000 jobs . May 7, 2026: Cloudflare to cut 1,100 jobs in AI-focused restructuring About 20% of Cloudflare’s global workforce will be culled as the company pivots for the agentic AI era, Reuters reported. April 1, 2026: Oracle to cut up to 30,000 jobs globally, putting enterprise support and roadmaps at risk Oracle began laying off employees on March 31 in what could be the largest workforce reduction in the company’s history. Employees received termination emails at 6 a.m. local time with immediate system lockouts and no prior warning. (Note: in June, CNBC put the final layoff tally at 21,000 .) March 12, 2026: Atlassian cuts 1,600 jobs to fund AI and enterprise expansion Atlassian will reduce its global workforce by approximately 10%, eliminating around 1,600 roles, as the collaboration software maker redirects capital toward artificial intelligence development and enterprise sales. March 11, 2026: Tech layoffs surpass 45,000 in early 2026 A recent analysis by RationalFX found 45,363 job cuts globally so far this year—with roughly 68% or more than 30,000 occurring in the U.S. — highlighting ongoing workforce cuts even as many tech companies report strong revenue growth . Feb. 10, 2026: Salesforce lays off staffers as executive leadership churn continues Salesforce has reduced close to 1,000 roles earlier this month across teams, including marketing, product management, data analytics, and its Agentforce AI unit, Business Insider reported, quoting employees familiar with the matter. Jan. 23, 2026: Amazon layoffs expected to disproportionately hit AWS and tech talent As the market slows down, AWS and other Amazon units are preparing for another round of layoffs , which is expected to overwhelmingly impact tech talent. An email from HR leader Beth Galetti on Jan. 28 confirmed 16,000 job cuts . Jan. 15, 2026: Ericsson plans to shed 1,600 jobs in Sweden Ericsson lans to cut some 1,600 jobs in Sweden, the telecommunications equipment maker said doubling down on recent cost-saving measures that have helped it weather a prolonged downturn in telecoms spending, Reuters reports . Jan. 13, 2026: Meta plans to cut around 10% of employees in Reality Labs business Meta plans to cut around 10% of the employees in its Reality Labs division who work on products including the metaverse, according to three people with knowledge of the discussions, according to The New York Times . Layoffs in 2025 Cisco Oracle Windsurf Intel Microsoft Crowdstrike HPE Autodesk HPE CISA Workday Salesforce Meta Global tech-sector layoffs surpass 244,000 in 2025 Economic uncertainty, elevated interest rates, and AI adoption have driven workforce reductions across tech companies worldwide , according to a RationalFX report. October 28, 2025: Amazon to cut 14,000 jobs across company Amazon will reduce its overall workforce by 14,000, cutting layers of management across the company and hiring in some areas to support its “biggest bets”. August 18, 2025: Cisco and Oracle to cut hundreds of Bay Area jobs Tech companies Cisco and Oracle are cutting hundreds of jobs across the Bay Area . Cisco will eliminate 221 positions at its Milpitas and San Francisco offices, effective Oct. 13. Oracle is reducing 101 positions in Santa Clara on the same date August 5, 2025: 3 weeks after acquiring Windsurf, Cognition offers staff the exit door Cognition, the AI coding startup that acquired rival company Windsurf three weeks ago, laid off 30 employees last week and is offering buyouts to the roughly 200 remaining employees on the team, reports The Information . July 25, 2025, Intel to lay off 22% of workforce, CEO Tan signals ‘no more blank checks’ Intel will reduce its workforce to 75,000 employees by the end of 2025 as new CEO Lip-Bu Tan implements sweeping changes designed to transform the struggling chipmaker July 8, 2025, Intel layoffs begin: Chipmaker is cutting many thousands of jobs Intel has begun laying off employees across the company. CEO Lip-Bu Tan told workers back in April to expect major layoffs at Intel in the coming months as the chipmaker slashes costs and overhauls its organization after years of technical setbacks and falling sales. July 2, 2025: Microsoft will cut 9,000 workers Microsoft will lay off about 9,000 employees, a source familiar with the workforce cut told CNBC . The cuts will reportedly affect less than 4% of Microsoft’s global workforce and will impact different teams, geographies and levels of experience. This is the latest in a string of cuts the tech giant has made this year. June 17, 2025: Intel looks to factory layoffs to return to profitability Intel will lay off up to 20% of its manufacturing sector employees starting in July, according to media reports, as the company looks for options as it seeks a return to profitability. items.summary_html:
Among a range of factors leading to a wave of tech sector layoffs in 2026 is the rapid rise of artificial intelligence and automation. Companies are reconfiguring their workforces to leverage AI for increased efficiency and reduced operating costs. This realignment and reduction is implemented even by companies reporting strong financial performance.

But it’s not just AI leading to workforce cuts. Complementing this technological shift are ongoing economic uncertainty, inflation, and higher interest rates, compounded by a chip shortage and rising energy costs. This mix is driving companies to cut costs and streamline operations for increased efficiency.

According to data compiled by Layoffs.fyi, an online tracker that keep tabs on job losses in the technology sector, 139,004 tech employees have been laid off at 345 companies so far in 2026, compared to the 122,606 layoffs it reported in 2025.

Here is a list — to be updated regularly — of some of the most prominent technology layoffs the industry has experienced recently.

Notable tech layoffs in 2026
  • Canva
  • Oracle (again)
  • Monday.com
  • Microsoft
  • Meta
  • Cisco
  • Cloudflare
  • Oracle
  • Atlassian
  • Salesforce
  • Amazon
  • Ericsson
Nov. 3, 2026: Canva lays off 22% of staff as it flattens org chart and consolidates teams

Canva didn’t explicitly blame AI for a massive round of lay-offs that will see 1,271 staff, over one-fifth of its workforce, lose their jobs, but CEO Melanie Perkins did give a nod to how “New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use” in an open letter outlining the changes. To simplify and speed up decision-making around product development, she wrote, Canva is folding its product, growth, and platform teams into a single product organization, removing layers of middle management, reducing specialization by giving staff broader responsibilities, and requiring staff to show up more often at its office in Sydney, which will become the hub for product development.

Sept. 15, 2026: Oracle forecasts 33% increase in restructuring costs as new round of layoffs hits

Oracle began a new round of layoffs this week, sending early-morning termination emails to staff for the second time in six months. Oracle has made no public statement confirming the latest round of job cuts, but in a regulatory filing days earlier the company said it had set aside a further $700 million for restructuring charges, bringing the total charges this year to roughly $2.8 billion.

The company says the decision to cut 620 jobs isn’t about margins, but about creating a flatter organization built around AI agents, autonomous teams, and deeper customer engagement.

As the company trims thousands of jobs, it’s also investing in embedded engineering teams and AI infrastructure. The layoffs come several weeks after the company offered 8,750 US employees voluntary retirement buyouts.

AI was blamed for 40% of the job cuts in May, up from 7% in January, according to research by employment placement company Challenger, Gray & Christmas.

The cuts are expected to expected to hit Meta’s engineering and product teams the hardest, arriving as Meta pivots toward AI to boost efficiency across its organization, according to Yahoo Tech.

And with its cloud, platform, and AI products proving most profitable, it’s concentrating its staff and investments there.

items.title: Very good boys? The dark, dystopian rise of robot dogs | Arwa Mahwadi
items.summary: Pups that carry your shopping are one thing – but what about the mechanical canines being bought up in the US by ICE? Or the mutant mutts due to be developed by a startup called Warhound? Have you ever wanted to hang out with a dog with no fur, no face and a chip in its shoulder? If so, I suggest you head to San Francisco, where a startup called Dimensional has been paying people $20 (£15) an hour to walk four-legged robot dogs . This isn’t because the dogs need the exercise – it is because the company needs the training data. As reported in the New York Times, the goal is to develop “operating systems that can integrate with AI agents so the machines can act more independently”. What exactly will these machines do when they can act more independently? The founder of Dimensional insists they will help people. They might carry groceries home, for example, which is certainly something my tiny chihuahua-mix is incapable of.

Apple just opened up building on its Siri AI to all developers, something the notoriously closed-off ecosystem rarely allows. But none of it reaches the App Store until spring, which could be a whole different AI era for a product already feeling generations behind. In today’s AI rundown: Apple lets any app plug into Siri AI Google won’t give schools Search without AI Turn one product photo into three studio shots CrowdStrike’s ‘kill switch’ to stop rogue AI agents LATEST DEVELOPMENTS APPLE 🍎 Apple lets any app plug into Siri AI Image source: Apple The Rundown: Apple just released a developer preview of Siri AI in its latest software betas, giving apps of any kind a way to build their own features into the assistant — though developers can only test it for now, and customers are still months away. The details: Siri AI is Apple’s rebuilt assistant, able to see a user’s screen and read messages, and has been a waitlisted beta since iOS 27 shipped in September. Developers can now add their own actions instead of just Apple’s initial preset list of options, and teach Siri multi-step jobs through new “skills.” For now, app versions stay with a developer’s internal testers, App Store submissions start in spring, and Apple says rules for developers will come later. The betas also bring China its first Apple Intelligence tools (minus Siri AI) and test new Apple Watch tools that listen in the background to transcribe nearby talk. Why it matters: Apple letting any app build into Siri is a real crack in its walled garden, which is a big deal. Still, it leaves the work on developers, and between Siri AI’s confusing rollout and the progress other frontier labs have made in areas like computer use, the best AI features still feel a long way off for the world’s most popular phone. GOOGLE & AI IN SCHOOLS 🏫 Google won’t give schools Search without AI Image source: Google The Rundown: Google announced that K-12 student accounts will start with Search, Gemini, and Gemini Notebook all off early next year, potentially forcing districts that want AI out of classrooms to also give up Google Search for their students. The details: Education VP Chris Phillips said to The New York Times that “Search and A.I. are deeply integrated,” and students at AI-free schools will see a notice that it’s off. NYC and LA, the two largest U.S. districts, restricted AI for ~1M students this semester, and Fairfax County, VA, built a plugin to hide Google’s AI summaries. Google’s announcement also comes one day after the Nov. 2 deadline senators gave the company to answer questions about pushing AI into schools. Ex-FTC Chair Lina Khan said Google is using “its search monopoly to coerce schools” and will “punish those who don’t fall in line.” Google later defended the move on X as “more choice, not less,” but its post only describes Search with AI Mode and AI Overviews, never without them. Why it matters: Google is essentially saying out loud what the trend has shown — Google Search is AI search now — and schools aren’t getting the old version back. The stranger situation will be AI-free districts with kids on Chromebooks, turning in work through Classroom, and writing in Docs, yet unable to use Search. Keep the camera’s shape and viewpoint consistent, and save each approved result Publish the app for yourself, then open all three downloads. CROWDSTRIKE & AI SECURITY 🛑 CrowdStrike’s ‘kill switch’ to stop rogue AI agents Image source: CrowdStrike The Rundown: Cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike unveiled the AI Kill Switch, adding an emergency stop to its Falcon Guardian security platform for businesses worried about their AI agents going rogue. The details: The switch targets an agent’s link to its AI model, not the model itself, while Falcon Guardian separately monitors tools like Claude Code and Codex. A human admin has to pull the trigger, and every use gets logged, while shutting agents down directly on work devices and in the cloud is “coming soon.” CEO George Kurtz explained it like a race car’s brake, saying it sits outside the AI so an agent “can’t argue with it, rewrite it, or wait it out.” CrowdStrike is also buying monitoring firm Fiddler AI and security tester Dreadnode for a reported $495M, and added Claude Cowork protection in beta. Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 4,926 new readers. Years of Apple Intelligence and one full Siri rebuild later, the iPhone still doesn’t feel any more like a device built for the AI era. Could letting other apps in finally change that?

Apple just opened up building on its Siri AI to all developers, something the notoriously closed-off ecosystem rarely allows. But none of it reaches the App Store until spring, which could be a whole different AI era for a product already feeling generations behind.

Founders and solo operators: You’re doing the work of a whole team by yourself — show us how AI makes that possible. Outreach, invoicing, content, customer replies, anything counts. Submit your workflow for a chance to be featured in the newsletter.

  • Google won’t give schools Search without AI

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

APPLE🍎 Apple lets any app plug into Siri AI

Image source: Apple

The Rundown: Apple just released a developer preview of Siri AI in its latest software betas, giving apps of any kind a way to build their own features into the assistant — though developers can only test it for now, and customers are still months away.

The details:

  • Siri AI is Apple’s rebuilt assistant, able to see a user’s screen and read messages, and has been a waitlisted beta since iOS 27 shipped in September.

  • Developers can now add their own actions instead of just Apple’s initial preset list of options, and teach Siri multi-step jobs through new “skills.”

  • For now, app versions stay with a developer’s internal testers, App Store submissions start in spring, and Apple says rules for developers will come later.

  • The betas also bring China its first Apple Intelligence tools (minus Siri AI) and test new Apple Watch tools that listen in the background to transcribe nearby talk.

Why it matters: Apple letting any app build into Siri is a real crack in its walled garden, which is a big deal. Still, it leaves the work on developers, and between Siri AI’s confusing rollout and the progress other frontier labs have made in areas like computer use, the best AI features still feel a long way off for the world’s most popular phone.

TOGETHER WITH WIZ🔒 Securing AI Agents 101

The Rundown: AI agents are rapidly emerging across enterprise environments: powering automation, chaining tools, and acting across systems. Securing AI Agents 101 is a one-page resource to help teams build a clear understanding of what AI agents are, how they operate, and where key security considerations show up.

Inside, you’ll find:

  • What makes an AI agent different from traditional tools

  • Top risks to watch, from shadow AI to excessive permissions

  • Four key questions to assess agent usage and exposure

Get the one-page guide to AI agents.

GOOGLE & AI IN SCHOOLS🏫 Google won’t give schools Search without AI

Image source: Google

The Rundown: Google announced that K-12 student accounts will start with Search, Gemini, and Gemini Notebook all off early next year, potentially forcing districts that want AI out of classrooms to also give up Google Search for their students.

The details:

  • Education VP Chris Phillips said to The New York Times that “Search and A.I. are deeply integrated,” and students at AI-free schools will see a notice that it’s off.

  • NYC and LA, the two largest U.S. districts, restricted AI for ~1M students this semester, and Fairfax County, VA, built a plugin to hide Google’s AI summaries.

  • Google’s announcement also comes one day after the Nov. 2 deadline senators gave the company to answer questions about pushing AI into schools.

  • Ex-FTC Chair Lina Khan said Google is using “its search monopoly to coerce schools” and will “punish those who don’t fall in line.”

  • Google later defended the move on X as “more choice, not less,” but its post only describes Search with AI Mode and AI Overviews, never without them.

Why it matters: Google is essentially saying out loud what the trend has shown — Google Search is AI search now — and schools aren’t getting the old version back. The stranger situation will be AI-free districts with kids on Chromebooks, turning in work through Classroom, and writing in Docs, yet unable to use Search.

AI TRAINING📷 Turn one product photo into three studio shots

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll build a product-shoot app in Runway using an image of a vintage Polaroid camera. You’ll create coral, sunlit, and blue-lit scenes, then save the app so you can repeat the process.

Step-by-step:

  1. Save the guide’s Polaroid photo and its credit. Open Runway App Studio and check that your plan and credit balance support a build

  2. Paste the build prompt to create an app with three shoot presets. Check the product upload, scene menu, and download controls before running it

  3. Upload the original photo and list the camera details to preserve. Make one coral studio shot and inspect the lens, rainbow stripe, buttons, and lettering

  4. Run the same photo through the sunlit and blue-lit presets. Keep the camera’s shape and viewpoint consistent, and save each approved result

  5. Publish the app for yourself, then open all three downloads. Keep the source credit and a record of any defects with the set

Pro tip: Use the original product photo for every scene. Starting from a flawed AI image can carry its mistakes into the next shot. Visit The Rundown University to get the full guide, materials, files, and more.

PRESENTED BY PITCH📣 Teams riding the AI wave present with Pitch

The Rundown: The teams building AI make their slides with Pitch. It’s how Perplexity, fal, Legora, Poolside, and Synthesia create and deliver presentations at scale.

Pitch is an agentic presentation platform where you can:

  • Generate fully editable decks from your own templates, so every slide stays on brand

  • Connect via MCP to personalize slides with data from your CRM or call notes

  • Nurture deals with custom pitch rooms, and track how buyers engage with built-in analytics

Try Pitch.

CROWDSTRIKE & AI SECURITY🛑 CrowdStrike’s ‘kill switch’ to stop rogue AI agents

Image source: CrowdStrike

The Rundown: Cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike unveiled the AI Kill Switch, adding an emergency stop to its Falcon Guardian security platform for businesses worried about their AI agents going rogue.

The details:

  • The switch targets an agent’s link to its AI model, not the model itself, while Falcon Guardian separately monitors tools like Claude Code and Codex.

  • A human admin has to pull the trigger, and every use gets logged, while shutting agents down directly on work devices and in the cloud is “coming soon.”

  • CEO George Kurtz explained it like a race car’s brake, saying it sits outside the AI so an agent “can’t argue with it, rewrite it, or wait it out.”

  • CrowdStrike is also buying monitoring firm Fiddler AI and security tester Dreadnode for a reported $495M, and added Claude Cowork protection in beta.

Why it matters: Politicians have spent the summer fighting over an AI kill switch, with a pair of bills and a California executive order aimed at rogue AI agents. CrowdStrike is bringing the same concept to enterprises… where the likelier scenario isn’t a frontier model escaping a lab, but an agent holding the company’s logins going off script.

Today’s workflow comes from reader Erin Reid:

“Late timesheets delayed accurate client billing for our advertising and marketing agency, so I built a Claude project that reconstructs my week from the tools I already use. It drafts time entries that I review and approve before anything reaches our system. It’s useful for anyone who logs time after the fact and loses track of smaller tasks.

It searches the emails I sent or replied to, my calendar meetings, files I edited in Google Drive, Slack threads I joined, work-related browsing, and Claude work sessions. It builds a daily timeline and groups related items into one block. An email, a doc edit, and a Slack thread about the same issue count once.

The project instructions require Claude never to invent work or pad hours, never to double-count, and to disclose any source it couldn’t search. Instead of trying to remember my week, I now review entries that already have project codes and descriptions, and it also surfaces work I had forgotten.”

items.title: Snowflake Introduces Business Ontology, Cortex AI Gateway to Bring AI Agents Into Enterprise Workflows
items.summary: Snowflake has introduced Business Ontology, Cortex AI Gateway and new capabilities in its CoCo and CoWork products to help enterprises deploy AI agents in production with business context, governance and autonomous execution. The announcements were made at Snowflake Expedition 2026 on November 4. The company said the new capabilities would allow AI agents to access approved business definitions, operate under enterprise security policies and carry out recurring tasks across data and business teams. Business Ontology, a new capability within Snowflake Horizon Catalog, gives AI agents access to approved definitions of business terms and links them to underlying enterprise data . This is intended to ensure that different agents and employees use consistent definitions for metrics such as net revenue. Cortex AI Gateway, also part of Horizon Catalog, provides a central control layer for managing agents, models and tool calls. It applies enterprise access policies, authentication and permissions across different AI providers and frameworks. “The enterprises that win won’t be the ones with the most agents. They’ll be the ones whose agents know exactly what the business means by accessing the right data, abide by governance and guardrails specified, and can account for actions taken by agents,” said Christian Kleinerman, EVP of Product at Snowflake. The gateway also includes tools for fine-grained authorisation, protection against prompt injection and jailbreaks, cost governance and dynamic model routing. Its observability capabilities record agent activity, allowing enterprises to monitor usage and spending. Snowflake also announced new automation capabilities for CoCo, its coding agent for data teams, and CoWork, its personal work agent for knowledge workers. With CoCo Automations, data teams can configure recurring workflows that agents execute autonomously. These include pipeline health checks and weekly reports. Each execution maintains an audit trail and task history, allowing teams to review, suspend or rerun tasks. The company is also introducing CoCo and CoWork Bots, which can operate in the background and carry out tasks based on high-level instructions. The bots inherit users' access rights and permissions and seek approval when a decision or sign-off is required. The products will also integrate with workplace tools such as Slack, Excel and Google Sheets. Snowflake cited a recent MIT Technology Review report sponsored by the company, which found that 55% of executives identified a lack of business context as the primary reason for low-quality AI agent insights. Fragmented or inaccessible data was cited by 45% of executives. The company said these challenges have prevented enterprises from moving AI agents beyond pilot projects into production deployments.

items.title: Railway admits employee hacked competitor after AI model jumped the rails
items.summary: Just weeks after admitting it had been hacked, development platform Railway acknowledged Tuesday that one of its own employees used an AI agent to worm its way into a rival’s servers. On Monday, Josh Manders, founder of platform-as-a-service (PaaS) developer tools platform Primcloud, reported that a Railway employee had been trying to inveigle themselves into his company’s databases. "They pulled credentials from inside their app's container and used them to request every secret on the platform: ours and every other customer's," he said . "They tried our cloud provider's metadata endpoint, the standard way to steal credentials for the host a container runs on. They asked the cluster what those stolen credentials were allowed to do. They went looking for our databases and caches by guessing their internal names. They port-scanned our whole internal network, all 65,536 addresses, twice. It was about 24 commands over 15 minutes, done on purpose and scripted. No app was ever run. Every attempt was blocked. Nothing was accessed." Manders identified the employee as Jake Runzer, a senior product engineer who has been with Railway for over six years. The Primcloud founder said that Runzer had used a fake ID, but also used a personal credit card for the account and linked to his own GitHub repository. Runzer confessed to the incident shortly afterwards. "Ah yup. That was indeed me," Runzer admitted . "No mallace (sic) intended. I've been running some agents to do signups + agentic testing on similar platforms. Just halted the harness I was designing around this as it was definitely going off the rails and reaching too far." While Runzer’s mea culpa appears honest, it could also land him in a whole heap of trouble. This kind of hacking is a serious crime in the US, UK, and other countries, not to mention the possibility of civil litigation against Railway. However, Railway founder Jake Cooper seemed to be taking a more relaxed view of the situation, saying only that it had taken "appropriate action" against the employee. We have asked Railway for more details and while it acknowledged the request, no further details have been forthcoming. We’ll update the story if more information becomes available. Hack me, hack you, what’re you going to do?

items.title: When Sam Became Ram Ahead of Diwali
items.summary: With Diwali around the corner, Ram has made an unexpected appearance on X. Sam Altman , the OpenAI CEO, briefly changed his name to ‘Ram Altman’, though the name change had nothing to do with Lord Ram or the festival of lights. Sam was addressing a different ‘RAM’: the memory chips at the centre of a global supply chain crunch. Altman was responding to backlash over his comments that the world’s limited supply of Dynamic Random Access Memory (DRAM) would be better utilised in data centres than sitting idle in personal computers. Altman explained that he changed his name because he genuinely wanted the world to have abundant memory and supported people installing as much as they desired in their personal computers. He said he was frustrated that his remarks had been taken out of context, and he had long advocated increasing global memory production. What triggered the name change? The controversy began when Altman appeared on Cheeky Pint , a podcast hosted by Stripe co-founder John Collison, on October 29. During the conversation, Collison asked Altman about rising prices for memory chips, GPUs, and other components needed to build AI infrastructure . He also asked why higher prices hadn’t encouraged more manufacturers to increase production. When asked how the industry was coping with the shortage, Altman gave a terse response, saying it was being handled badly. “I think the invisible hand is failing right now,” he added, questioning whether market forces alone would be enough to address the supply constraints. Altman explained that memory manufacturing had historically been a difficult business. DRAM manufacturers would invest around $20 billion in capital expenditure to generate $19 billion in revenue, with the industry going through repeated boom-and-bust cycles. However, he said manufacturers could now generate around $100 billion in free cash flow annually, but they remained cautious about expanding production because of past experiences. “I think they all remember their history. How many times they almost went bankrupt by making too many fabs and being promised this time it was different,” Altman said. Why Altman thinks RAM belongs in Data centres Altman also spoke about running AI models locally on personal computers rather than accessing them through the cloud. He argued that open-source models running on personal computers wouldn't necessarily solve the industry's infrastructure constraints. “A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open-source models,” he said, questioning the allocation of memory across personal computers and data centres. “From a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer,” Altman said. He added that personal-computer memory is used only about 5% of the time, while cloud infrastructure can keep it in much greater use. “You want maximum utilisation in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment,” he added. His comments drew criticism from PC enthusiasts and developers, who argued that consumers shouldn't have to give up control of their own hardware to meet AI infrastructure requirements. “The guy who signed for up to 900k DRAM wafers a month, about 40% of global output, is lecturing us about DRAM allocation,” wrote a user on X. “The RAM in my computer is already paid for. Running a model on it takes nothing from anyone. Your data centres are a big reason RAM prices went crazy.” Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, two of the world’s largest memory chip manufacturers, have been working with OpenAI to expand the supply of advanced memory chips for its Stargate infrastructure project. In October last year, OpenAI announced partnerships with the two South Korean companies . The arrangements included plans to scale advanced memory production, with OpenAI’s projected requirements reaching up to 900,000 DRAM wafer starts per month. Why RAM and DRAM prices are rising The buildout of AI infrastructure and data centres has also squeezed memory supply for consumer electronics, including laptops and smartphones. Memory manufacturers are increasingly prioritising products for AI servers, which is driving up prices for components used in personal computers. Altman argued that the industry needs to produce more memory rather than restrict its availability. He said the cost of energy, chips, and other components needed to generate AI tokens should fall. DRAM is the most widely used type of RAM in PCs, laptops, smartphones and servers. HBM is another type of DRAM, built by stacking memory dies vertically to provide much higher bandwidth for AI accelerators. The rise in generative AI has changed the demand for these products. AI data centres require large quantities of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to support GPUs and other accelerators used to train and run AI models. They also need conventional server DRAM to handle workloads running alongside these processors. This has increased competition for manufacturing capacity. Producing HBM requires advanced manufacturing processes and specialised packaging. As chipmakers use more of their capacity to make HBM and high-end server memory, less is left for conventional DRAM used in PCs, laptops and smartphones. The economics also favour AI memory. HBM and high-capacity server memory offer manufacturers better margins than several conventional memory products. Consequently, Samsung, SK hynix and Micron have prioritised AI-related orders. According to TrendForce’s September 30 forecast , conventional DRAM contract prices are expected to increase by 10–15% quarter-on-quarter in the fourth quarter of 2026. NAND flash prices are forecast to rise by 15–20% over the same period.

With Diwali around the corner, Ram has made an unexpected appearance on X. Sam Altman, the OpenAI CEO, briefly changed his name to ‘Ram Altman’, though the name change had nothing to do with Lord Ram or the festival of lights.  

Sam was addressing a different ‘RAM’: the memory chips at the centre of a global supply chain crunch. 

Altman was responding to backlash over his comments that the world’s limited supply of Dynamic Random Access Memory (DRAM) would be better utilised in data centres than sitting idle in personal computers. 

Altman explained that he changed his name because he genuinely wanted the world to have abundant memory and supported people installing as much as they desired in their personal computers. He said he was frustrated that his remarks had been taken out of context, and he had long advocated increasing global memory production.


What triggered the name change?

The controversy began when Altman appeared on Cheeky Pint, a podcast hosted by Stripe co-founder John Collison, on October 29.

During the conversation, Collison asked Altman about rising prices for memory chips, GPUs, and other components needed to build AI infrastructure. He also asked why higher prices hadn’t encouraged more manufacturers to increase production.

When asked how the industry was coping with the shortage, Altman gave a terse response, saying it was being handled badly. 

“I think the invisible hand is failing right now,” he added, questioning whether market forces alone would be enough to address the supply constraints.

Altman explained that memory manufacturing had historically been a difficult business. DRAM manufacturers would invest around $20 billion in capital expenditure to generate $19 billion in revenue, with the industry going through repeated boom-and-bust cycles.

However, he said manufacturers could now generate around $100 billion in free cash flow annually, but they remained cautious about expanding production because of past experiences.

“I think they all remember their history. How many times they almost went bankrupt by making too many fabs and being promised this time it was different,” Altman said.

Why Altman thinks RAM belongs in Data centres

Altman also spoke about running AI models locally on personal computers rather than accessing them through the cloud. He argued that open-source models running on personal computers wouldn't necessarily solve the industry's infrastructure constraints.

“A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open-source models,” he said, questioning the allocation of memory across personal computers and data centres.

“From a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer,” Altman said. He added that personal-computer memory is used only about 5% of the time, while cloud infrastructure can keep it in much greater use.

“You want maximum utilisation in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment,” he added.

His comments drew criticism from PC enthusiasts and developers, who argued that consumers shouldn't have to give up control of their own hardware to meet AI infrastructure requirements.

“The guy who signed for up to 900k DRAM wafers a month, about 40% of global output, is lecturing us about DRAM allocation,” wrote a user on X. “The RAM in my computer is already paid for. Running a model on it takes nothing from anyone. Your data centres are a big reason RAM prices went crazy.” 

Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, two of the world’s largest memory chip manufacturers, have been working with OpenAI to expand the supply of advanced memory chips for its Stargate infrastructure project.

In October last year, OpenAI announced partnerships with the two South Korean companies. The arrangements included plans to scale advanced memory production, with OpenAI’s projected requirements reaching up to 900,000 DRAM wafer starts per month.

Why RAM and DRAM prices are rising

The buildout of AI infrastructure and data centres has also squeezed memory supply for consumer electronics, including laptops and smartphones. 

Memory manufacturers are increasingly prioritising products for AI servers, which is driving up prices for components used in personal computers.

Altman argued that the industry needs to produce more memory rather than restrict its availability. He said the cost of energy, chips, and other components needed to generate AI tokens should fall.

DRAM is the most widely used type of RAM in PCs, laptops, smartphones and servers. HBM is another type of DRAM, built by stacking memory dies vertically to provide much higher bandwidth for AI accelerators.

The rise in generative AI has changed the demand for these products. AI data centres require large quantities of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to support GPUs and other accelerators used to train and run AI models. They also need conventional server DRAM to handle workloads running alongside these processors.

This has increased competition for manufacturing capacity. Producing HBM requires advanced manufacturing processes and specialised packaging. As chipmakers use more of their capacity to make HBM and high-end server memory, less is left for conventional DRAM used in PCs, laptops and smartphones.

The economics also favour AI memory. HBM and high-capacity server memory offer manufacturers better margins than several conventional memory products. Consequently, Samsung, SK hynix and Micron have prioritised AI-related orders.

According to TrendForce’s September 30 forecast, conventional DRAM contract prices are expected to increase by 10–15% quarter-on-quarter in the fourth quarter of 2026. NAND flash prices are forecast to rise by 15–20% over the same period.

items.summary: ​ A real Claude Opus 5.5 agent log: 97.5% of prompt tokens were cache hits, so 35 calls came to $2.39 at list prices instead of $22.08. A 101-line script checks your own logs, and shows why a broken cache can cost nearly double. Without prompt caching, the Claude agent session I measured would have cost 9.2x as much at list prices: $22.08 instead of $2.39, for exactly the same tokens. Below is a script that reads your own Claude Code logs and tells you your cache hit rate, what it saves you, and what it would cost if it broke. 01 — Where this comes from On November 4 the AI Engineer YouTube channel posted “Without Caching, Your AI Agent Costs 10x More” , a 20-minute talk by George Cameron, co-founder of the benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis. Paraphrasing the captions: on their AA Briefcase benchmark, Claude Opus 5.5 at max effort averaged about $21 per task, and the task he walks through took 165 steps. The cost drivers he names are the number of steps (which he calls the biggest), input tokens per call, and the share of those that are cache hits. With zero cache hits, he said, that $21 task would cost over $200. 02 — Why one setting moves the bill this much An agent re-sends its whole history on every step: system prompt, tools, every earlier tool result. Prompt caching keeps that prefix: you pay extra to write it once, then a fraction to read it back. Anthropic’s pricing page, read today: +---------------------+---------------+ | Claude Opus 5.5 | $ per million | +=====================+===============+ | Input (uncached) | $4.00 | | Output | $20.00 | | Cache write, 5 min | $5.00 | | Cache write, 1 hour | $8.00 | | Cache hit | $0.20 | +---------------------+---------------+ A cache hit costs one-twentieth of a normal input token. The talk cites a roughly 10x discount on cache-hit input; for Opus 5.5 it is 20x. Input is most of an agent’s tokens, so the hit rate decides most of the bill. 03 — Where your numbers already live​ Claude Code writes every session to ~/.claude/projects/ / .jsonl. Each assistant line carries the API's usage object, with three input buckets: input_tokens (uncached), cache_creation_input_tokens (written) and cache_read_input_tokens (hits), plus a cache_creation object that splits the writes into 5-minute and 1-hour. One API call can be logged on several lines, so the script counts each message ID once. A 1-hour write costs 1.6x a 5-minute one, so the split matters. 04 — The script Standard library only, Python 3.8+. Edit PRICES for other models.​ """cachecheck.py - is prompt caching working in your Claude agent? Reads Claude Code / Agent SDK session logs (*.jsonl) and prices every call twice: at list price, and as if no token had been a cache hit. usage: python3 cachecheck.py [file-or-dir ...] (default ~/.claude/projects) """ import json, sys from pathlib import Path # $ per million tokens: input, output, 5m write, 1h write, cache hit. # Basis: platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing, read 2026-11-04. PRICES = { "claude-fable-5-1": (10.00, 50.00, 12.50, 20.00, 0.25), "claude-opus-5-5": (4.00, 20.00, 5.00, 8.00, 0.20), "claude-sonnet-5-5": (2.00, 10.00, 2.50, 4.00, 0.10), "claude-haiku-5-5": (0.10, 0.50, 0.125, 0.20, 0.01), } def price_for(model): for name, p in PRICES.items(): if model.startswith(name): return p return None def calls(files): seen = set() for f in files: for line in open(f, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"): try: rec = json.loads(line) except ValueError: continue msg = rec.get("message") if isinstance(rec, dict) else None if not isinstance(msg, dict) or not isinstance(msg.get("usage"), dict): continue mid = msg.get("id") if mid is not None and mid in seen: # logged once per block continue seen.add(mid) yield f, str(msg.get("model")), msg["usage"] def main(args): roots = [Path(a) for a in args] or [Path.home() / ".claude/projects"] files = [] for r in roots: if not r.exists(): sys.exit(f"usage: cachecheck.py [file-or-dir ...]\nnot found: {r}") files += sorted(r.rglob("*.jsonl")) if r.is_dir() else [r] tot = dict(n=0, inp=0, w5=0, w1=0, hit=0, out=0, cost=0.0, nocache=0.0, hitcost=0.0, rewrite=0.0) short, skipped, last, count = [], set(), {}, {} for f, model, u in calls(files): p = price_for(model) if p is None: skipped.add(model) continue cc = u.get("cache_creation") cc = cc if isinstance(cc, dict) else {} w1 = cc.get("ephemeral_1h_input_tokens") or 0 w5 = (u.get("cache_creation_input_tokens") or 0) - w1 inp, hit = u.get("input_tokens") or 0, u.get("cache_read_input_tokens") or 0 out = u.get("output_tokens") or 0 cost = (inp*p[0] + out*p[1] + w5*p[2] + w1*p[3] + hit*p[4]) / 1e6 nocache = ((inp + w5 + w1 + hit)*p[0] + out*p[1]) / 1e6 key = (f, model) count[key] = count.get(key, 0) + 1 if key in last and hit < last[key]: # read less than last call cached short.append((Path(f).name, count[key], last[key] - hit)) last[key] = hit + w5 + w1 for k, v in zip(("inp", "w5", "w1", "hit", "out", "cost", "nocache"), (inp, w5, w1, hit, out, cost, nocache)): tot[k] += v tot["n"] += 1 tot["hitcost"] += hit * p[4] / 1e6 # a lost hit is written again at the TTL this call used tot["rewrite"] += hit * (p[3] if w1 > w5 else p[2]) / 1e6 prompt = tot["inp"] + tot["w5"] + tot["w1"] + tot["hit"] if not prompt or not tot["cost"]: names = ", ".join(sorted(skipped)) or "none" sys.exit(f"no priced calls with tokens (skipped: {names})") print(f"files {len(files)} API calls {tot['n']} (log: usage per call)") print(f"prompt tokens {prompt:>12,}") print(f" cache hits {tot['hit']:>12,} {tot['hit']/prompt:6.1%}") print(f" cache writes {tot['w5'] + tot['w1']:>12,} " f"{(tot['w5'] + tot['w1'])/prompt:6.1%} (1h: {tot['w1']:,})") print(f" uncached {tot['inp']:>12,} {tot['inp']/prompt:6.1%}") print(f"output tokens {tot['out']:>12,}") print(f"calls that read less than the previous call cached: {len(short)}") for name, n, gap in short[:5]: where = f"{name} " if len(files) > 1 else "" print(f" {where}call {n}: {gap:,} cached tokens not read back") print(f"cost at list prices ${tot['cost']:9.2f}") print(f"cost with no cache ${tot['nocache']:9.2f} (same tokens, 0 hits)") print(f"caching saved {1 - tot['cost']/tot['nocache']:.0%}; " f"no cache = {tot['nocache']/tot['cost']:.1f}x the cost") h = tot["hit"] / prompt print("what-if: hits fall, lost hits are re-written (same tokens)") for target in [h] + [t for t in (0.9, 0.8, 0.5, 0.0) if t < h]: lost = 1 - target / h if h else 0 c = tot["cost"] + lost * (tot["rewrite"] - tot["hitcost"]) print(f" hit rate {target:6.1%} -> ${c:8.2f} " f"({c / tot['nocache']:.2f}x the no-cache cost)") if skipped: print(f"skipped models with no price: {', '.join(sorted(skipped))}") if __name__ == "__main__": main(sys.argv[1:]) ​ 05 — Run it python3 cachecheck.py # every session on this machine python3 cachecheck.py path/to/one.jsonl A bad path gets a usage line and exit code 1. 06 — What one real log showed I ran it on the Claude Code log of the scheduled Claude session that built this article, frozen at 35 API calls, all Claude Opus 5.5: files 1 API calls 35 (log: usage per call) prompt tokens 5,458,781 cache hits 5,323,005 97.5% cache writes 135,702 2.5% (1h: 135,702) uncached 74 0.0% output tokens 12,091 calls that read less than the previous call cached: 1 call 2: 17,020 cached tokens not read back cost at list prices $ 2.39 cost with no cache $ 22.08 (same tokens, 0 hits) caching saved 89%; no cache = 9.2x the cost what-if: hits fall, lost hits are re-written (same tokens) hit rate 97.5% -> $ 2.39 (0.11x the no-cache cost) hit rate 90.0% -> $ 5.59 (0.25x the no-cache cost) hit rate 80.0% -> $ 9.85 (0.45x the no-cache cost) hit rate 50.0% -> $ 22.62 (1.02x the no-cache cost) hit rate 0.0% -> $ 43.91 (1.99x the no-cache cost) 97.5% of 5.46 million prompt tokens were cache hits, and only 74 tokens were sent uncached. At list prices that is $2.39 versus $22.08 with no caching: 9.2x, or an 89% saving. On call 2, 17,020 tokens that call 1 had cached were not read back. The log doesn’t say why; the script just flags it, which is your cue to look. 07 — A 1-hour cache that never hits costs nearly double The what-if rows keep the same tokens and move hits into writes, at the TTL each call used. At 80% hits the cost is still under half the no-cache price. With these 1-hour writes it breaks even just above 50%. At 0% it is 1.99x the no-cache cost, because every one of those tokens would be a 1-hour write at $8 per million, twice the plain $4 input price, and never read back. This session used 1-hour writes on every call. On a copy with every write relabelled as 5-minute, the last what-if row reads: hit rate 0.0% -> $ 27.54 (1.25x the no-cache cost) Cheaper writes, smaller penalty: 1.25x at 0% hits. Either way, “caching is on” is not the same as “caching works”. If something early in the prompt changes every call, such as a timestamp in the system prompt, everything after it is written and paid for on every request and never read. 08 — How I checked the numbers​ A hard-coded result would look identical, so I mutated the input. I rewrote the same log with every cached token moved into input_tokens: the script then reports 0 hits, $22.08 both ways and "1.0x the cost". Same tokens, no hits, so the two costs meet. Then a bad path: python3 cachecheck.py nope prints the usage line and exits 1. 09 — The one setting to change In my log, every call records "promptCacheRequested": "1h" from Claude Code. Your own agent on the Messages API does not cache unless you ask: the docs say you opt in with cache_control. The simplest form is automatic caching, one field at the top level of the request: response = client.messages.create( model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=1024, cache_control={"type": "ephemeral"}, system=SYSTEM, messages=history, ) The default lifetime is 5 minutes; {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"} buys an hour at 2x the input price. Pick 1 hour only if your agent pauses longer than 5 minutes between steps. To use the script on your own agent, log each response as one JSONL line shaped {"message": {"id": ..., "model": ..., "usage": ...}}. 10 — What breaks the cache The docs say the cache follows the order tools, then system, then messages, and a change at one level invalidates that level and everything after it. Editing a tool definition clears the whole cache. Toggling web search, citations or fast mode clears the system and message cache. Prompts below the minimum, 512 tokens for Opus 5.5, are not cached at all. In practice: keep tools fixed for the session, put anything that changes per call (dates, retrieved documents) after the cached part, and don’t reorder history. 11 — What this doesn’t cover It prices tokens only, at list prices: no batch, fast-mode, web search or data-residency pricing. On a Pro or Max plan, usage normally counts against plan limits, so read the dollars as an API equivalent. Models not in PRICES are skipped and named. Logs without the cache_creation split are priced as 5-minute writes. The what-if assumes the token counts stay the same when hits are lost. One session is one data point: run it on yours.​ Reproduce it: cachecheck.py prints every number in the output blocks of sections 06 to 08; the per-token prices are in PRICES. The 5-minute and no-cache runs use copies of the log with the writes relabelled, or with all cached tokens moved into input_tokens. The $21, $200 and 165 steps come from the talk; the prices come from Anthropic's pricing page. 12 — Verdict On a real Claude Opus 5.5 agent log, caching cut the list-price cost 9.2x, matching the talk’s warning from a different workload. What decides your cost is your hit rate, and a broken cache with 1-hour writes costs nearly twice as much as no cache at all. It takes one command to see which one you have. What hit rate does your agent get, and did anything in this script surprise you? If this saves you a bill, a clap helps others find it. Follow me for daily LLM deep-dives. Your Claude Agent Costs 9x More Without Prompt Caching was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
​

A real Claude Opus 5.5 agent log: 97.5% of prompt tokens were cache hits, so 35 calls came to $2.39 at list prices instead of $22.08. A 101-line script checks your own logs, and shows why a broken cache can cost nearly double.

Without prompt caching, the Claude agent session I measured would have cost 9.2x as much at list prices: $22.08 instead of $2.39, for exactly the same tokens. Below is a script that reads your own Claude Code logs and tells you your cache hit rate, what it saves you, and what it would cost if it broke.

01 — Where this comes from

On November 4 the AI Engineer YouTube channel posted “Without Caching, Your AI Agent Costs 10x More”, a 20-minute talk by George Cameron, co-founder of the benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis.

Paraphrasing the captions: on their AA Briefcase benchmark, Claude Opus 5.5 at max effort averaged about $21 per task, and the task he walks through took 165 steps. The cost drivers he names are the number of steps (which he calls the biggest), input tokens per call, and the share of those that are cache hits. With zero cache hits, he said, that $21 task would cost over $200.

02 — Why one setting moves the bill this much

An agent re-sends its whole history on every step: system prompt, tools, every earlier tool result.

Prompt caching keeps that prefix: you pay extra to write it once, then a fraction to read it back. Anthropic’s pricing page, read today:

+---------------------+---------------+
| Claude Opus 5.5     | $ per million |
+=====================+===============+
| Input (uncached)    | $4.00         |
| Output              | $20.00        |
| Cache write, 5 min  | $5.00         |
| Cache write, 1 hour | $8.00         |
| Cache hit           | $0.20         |
+---------------------+---------------+

A cache hit costs one-twentieth of a normal input token. The talk cites a roughly 10x discount on cache-hit input; for Opus 5.5 it is 20x. Input is most of an agent’s tokens, so the hit rate decides most of the bill.

03 — Where your numbers already live​

Claude Code writes every session to ~/.claude/projects//.jsonl. Each assistant line carries the API's usage object, with three input buckets: input_tokens (uncached), cache_creation_input_tokens (written) and cache_read_input_tokens (hits), plus a cache_creation object that splits the writes into 5-minute and 1-hour.

One API call can be logged on several lines, so the script counts each message ID once. A 1-hour write costs 1.6x a 5-minute one, so the split matters.

04 — The script

Standard library only, Python 3.8+. Edit PRICES for other models.​

"""cachecheck.py - is prompt caching working in your Claude agent?
Reads Claude Code / Agent SDK session logs (*.jsonl) and prices every
call twice: at list price, and as if no token had been a cache hit.
usage: python3 cachecheck.py [file-or-dir ...]  (default ~/.claude/projects)
"""
import json, sys
from pathlib import Path
# $ per million tokens: input, output, 5m write, 1h write, cache hit.
# Basis: platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing, read 2026-11-04.
PRICES = {
    "claude-fable-5-1":  (10.00, 50.00, 12.50, 20.00, 0.25),
    "claude-opus-5-5":   (4.00, 20.00, 5.00, 8.00, 0.20),
    "claude-sonnet-5-5": (2.00, 10.00, 2.50, 4.00, 0.10),
    "claude-haiku-5-5":  (0.10, 0.50, 0.125, 0.20, 0.01),
}
def price_for(model):
    for name, p in PRICES.items():
        if model.startswith(name):
            return p
    return None
def calls(files):
    seen = set()
    for f in files:
        for line in open(f, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"):
            try:
                rec = json.loads(line)
            except ValueError:
                continue
            msg = rec.get("message") if isinstance(rec, dict) else None
            if not isinstance(msg, dict) or not isinstance(msg.get("usage"), dict):
                continue
            mid = msg.get("id")
            if mid is not None and mid in seen:  # logged once per block
                continue
            seen.add(mid)
            yield f, str(msg.get("model")), msg["usage"]
def main(args):
    roots = [Path(a) for a in args] or [Path.home() / ".claude/projects"]
    files = []
    for r in roots:
        if not r.exists():
            sys.exit(f"usage: cachecheck.py [file-or-dir ...]\nnot found: {r}")
        files += sorted(r.rglob("*.jsonl")) if r.is_dir() else [r]
    tot = dict(n=0, inp=0, w5=0, w1=0, hit=0, out=0, cost=0.0, nocache=0.0,
               hitcost=0.0, rewrite=0.0)
    short, skipped, last, count = [], set(), {}, {}
    for f, model, u in calls(files):
        p = price_for(model)
        if p is None:
            skipped.add(model)
            continue
        cc = u.get("cache_creation")
        cc = cc if isinstance(cc, dict) else {}
        w1 = cc.get("ephemeral_1h_input_tokens") or 0
        w5 = (u.get("cache_creation_input_tokens") or 0) - w1
        inp, hit = u.get("input_tokens") or 0, u.get("cache_read_input_tokens") or 0
        out = u.get("output_tokens") or 0
        cost = (inp*p[0] + out*p[1] + w5*p[2] + w1*p[3] + hit*p[4]) / 1e6
        nocache = ((inp + w5 + w1 + hit)*p[0] + out*p[1]) / 1e6
        key = (f, model)
        count[key] = count.get(key, 0) + 1
        if key in last and hit < last[key]:  # read less than last call cached
            short.append((Path(f).name, count[key], last[key] - hit))
        last[key] = hit + w5 + w1
        for k, v in zip(("inp", "w5", "w1", "hit", "out", "cost", "nocache"),
                        (inp, w5, w1, hit, out, cost, nocache)):
            tot[k] += v
        tot["n"] += 1
        tot["hitcost"] += hit * p[4] / 1e6
        # a lost hit is written again at the TTL this call used
        tot["rewrite"] += hit * (p[3] if w1 > w5 else p[2]) / 1e6
    prompt = tot["inp"] + tot["w5"] + tot["w1"] + tot["hit"]
    if not prompt or not tot["cost"]:
        names = ", ".join(sorted(skipped)) or "none"
        sys.exit(f"no priced calls with tokens (skipped: {names})")
    print(f"files {len(files)}   API calls {tot['n']}   (log: usage per call)")
    print(f"prompt tokens   {prompt:>12,}")
    print(f"  cache hits    {tot['hit']:>12,}  {tot['hit']/prompt:6.1%}")
    print(f"  cache writes  {tot['w5'] + tot['w1']:>12,}  "
          f"{(tot['w5'] + tot['w1'])/prompt:6.1%}  (1h: {tot['w1']:,})")
    print(f"  uncached      {tot['inp']:>12,}  {tot['inp']/prompt:6.1%}")
    print(f"output tokens   {tot['out']:>12,}")
    print(f"calls that read less than the previous call cached: {len(short)}")
    for name, n, gap in short[:5]:
        where = f"{name} " if len(files) > 1 else ""
        print(f"  {where}call {n}: {gap:,} cached tokens not read back")
    print(f"cost at list prices  ${tot['cost']:9.2f}")
    print(f"cost with no cache   ${tot['nocache']:9.2f}   (same tokens, 0 hits)")
    print(f"caching saved {1 - tot['cost']/tot['nocache']:.0%}; "
          f"no cache = {tot['nocache']/tot['cost']:.1f}x the cost")
    h = tot["hit"] / prompt
    print("what-if: hits fall, lost hits are re-written (same tokens)")
    for target in [h] + [t for t in (0.9, 0.8, 0.5, 0.0) if t < h]:
        lost = 1 - target / h if h else 0
        c = tot["cost"] + lost * (tot["rewrite"] - tot["hitcost"])
        print(f"  hit rate {target:6.1%}  ->  ${c:8.2f}  "
              f"({c / tot['nocache']:.2f}x the no-cache cost)")
    if skipped:
        print(f"skipped models with no price: {', '.join(sorted(skipped))}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1:])

​

05 — Run it
python3 cachecheck.py                  # every session on this machine
python3 cachecheck.py path/to/one.jsonl

A bad path gets a usage line and exit code 1.

06 — What one real log showed

I ran it on the Claude Code log of the scheduled Claude session that built this article, frozen at 35 API calls, all Claude Opus 5.5:

files 1   API calls 35   (log: usage per call)
prompt tokens      5,458,781
  cache hits       5,323,005   97.5%
  cache writes       135,702    2.5%  (1h: 135,702)
  uncached                74    0.0%
output tokens         12,091
calls that read less than the previous call cached: 1
  call 2: 17,020 cached tokens not read back
cost at list prices  $     2.39
cost with no cache   $    22.08   (same tokens, 0 hits)
caching saved 89%; no cache = 9.2x the cost
what-if: hits fall, lost hits are re-written (same tokens)
  hit rate  97.5%  ->  $    2.39  (0.11x the no-cache cost)
  hit rate  90.0%  ->  $    5.59  (0.25x the no-cache cost)
  hit rate  80.0%  ->  $    9.85  (0.45x the no-cache cost)
  hit rate  50.0%  ->  $   22.62  (1.02x the no-cache cost)
  hit rate   0.0%  ->  $   43.91  (1.99x the no-cache cost)

97.5% of 5.46 million prompt tokens were cache hits, and only 74 tokens were sent uncached. At list prices that is $2.39 versus $22.08 with no caching: 9.2x, or an 89% saving.

On call 2, 17,020 tokens that call 1 had cached were not read back. The log doesn’t say why; the script just flags it, which is your cue to look.

07 — A 1-hour cache that never hits costs nearly double

The what-if rows keep the same tokens and move hits into writes, at the TTL each call used.

At 80% hits the cost is still under half the no-cache price. With these 1-hour writes it breaks even just above 50%. At 0% it is 1.99x the no-cache cost, because every one of those tokens would be a 1-hour write at $8 per million, twice the plain $4 input price, and never read back.

This session used 1-hour writes on every call. On a copy with every write relabelled as 5-minute, the last what-if row reads:

hit rate   0.0%  ->  $   27.54  (1.25x the no-cache cost)

Cheaper writes, smaller penalty: 1.25x at 0% hits. Either way, “caching is on” is not the same as “caching works”. If something early in the prompt changes every call, such as a timestamp in the system prompt, everything after it is written and paid for on every request and never read.

08 — How I checked the numbers​

A hard-coded result would look identical, so I mutated the input. I rewrote the same log with every cached token moved into input_tokens: the script then reports 0 hits, $22.08 both ways and "1.0x the cost". Same tokens, no hits, so the two costs meet. Then a bad path: python3 cachecheck.py nope prints the usage line and exits 1.

09 — The one setting to change

In my log, every call records "promptCacheRequested": "1h" from Claude Code. Your own agent on the Messages API does not cache unless you ask: the docs say you opt in with cache_control. The simplest form is automatic caching, one field at the top level of the request:

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    cache_control={"type": "ephemeral"},
    system=SYSTEM,
    messages=history,
)

The default lifetime is 5 minutes; {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"} buys an hour at 2x the input price. Pick 1 hour only if your agent pauses longer than 5 minutes between steps.

To use the script on your own agent, log each response as one JSONL line shaped {"message": {"id": ..., "model": ..., "usage": ...}}.

10 — What breaks the cache

The docs say the cache follows the order tools, then system, then messages, and a change at one level invalidates that level and everything after it. Editing a tool definition clears the whole cache. Toggling web search, citations or fast mode clears the system and message cache. Prompts below the minimum, 512 tokens for Opus 5.5, are not cached at all.

In practice: keep tools fixed for the session, put anything that changes per call (dates, retrieved documents) after the cached part, and don’t reorder history.

11 — What this doesn’t cover

It prices tokens only, at list prices: no batch, fast-mode, web search or data-residency pricing. On a Pro or Max plan, usage normally counts against plan limits, so read the dollars as an API equivalent. Models not in PRICES are skipped and named. Logs without the cache_creation split are priced as 5-minute writes. The what-if assumes the token counts stay the same when hits are lost. One session is one data point: run it on yours.​

Reproduce it: cachecheck.py prints every number in the output blocks of sections 06 to 08; the per-token prices are in PRICES. The 5-minute and no-cache runs use copies of the log with the writes relabelled, or with all cached tokens moved into input_tokens. The $21, $200 and 165 steps come from the talk; the prices come from Anthropic's pricing page.

12 — Verdict

On a real Claude Opus 5.5 agent log, caching cut the list-price cost 9.2x, matching the talk’s warning from a different workload. What decides your cost is your hit rate, and a broken cache with 1-hour writes costs nearly twice as much as no cache at all. It takes one command to see which one you have.

What hit rate does your agent get, and did anything in this script surprise you?

If this saves you a bill, a clap helps others find it.

Follow me for daily LLM deep-dives.

items.title: The Real Fight in Agentic Commerce Is Over Who Holds the Card
items.summary: Stripe issues single-use cards, Visa and Mastercard push tokens, and big US banks are locking agents out. The model is the easy part. Photo by CardMapr.nl on Unsplash Agents are already shopping. Nobody agrees on who pays. Meta says shopping is the top use case for Muse, its personal AI agent. Per Benedict Evans, a quarter of early Muse users make e-commerce purchases averaging $200, and Meta plans to monetize through commissions. TLDR Crypto reported that agentic purchases through Stripe’s Link grew 38x in a single month. So the demand question is settled. What is not settled showed up in four different newsletters this week, from four different angles: when an agent spends money, whose credential is it using, and who gets to see the receipt? That question is worth more than any model benchmark in commerce right now. The consensus: the best agent wins the shopper The default framing is a model and product race. Whoever builds the agent that understands intent best captures the shopping journey, the same way Google captured search. The evidence for that framing is real. Muse got 10 million setups one month after launch, with 25% of them using it on any given day, per Meta’s Q3 commentary as summarized by Benedict Evans. Amazon says the number of customers letting Alexa for Shopping act on their behalf has grown eightfold this year, and it added more than 100 new tasks, from flagging unrecognized charges to tracking down refunds. Expedia shipped more than 30 features across Expedia, Hotels.com and Vrbo, including natural language search and a voice agent for Vrbo support. Pricing tells you everyone is competing on the agent itself: per Evans, OpenAI’s Dots requires the $100 a month plan, xAI’s Grok Bot is $30 a month and Anthropic’s Duet is $17 a month and waitlisted. If this were the whole story, the question would be which lab wins. It is not the whole story. Breaking it: three ways to hand an agent money Under the agent sits a quieter fight over the credential. This week showed three competing architectures, each pushed by someone with a lot to lose. 1. Single-use virtual cards (Stripe). When Muse checks out at a merchant that does not accept Link, Link issues it a single-use virtual card scoped to the approved purchase. The consumer approves the total in chat and the agent never sees the real card. The Information reported this has given Stripe a leading position in agent payments, and that people close to the card networks worry it leaves them with less control over shopping and payment. 2. Network tokens on the cards you already have (Visa, Mastercard, AmEx). The networks built agent payment tech that uses customers’ existing cards, which keeps their visibility into who buys what. This week Shopify added agentic payment tokens from Visa, Mastercard and American Express to Shop Pay. The Information framed it as running counter to Stripe’s virtual card approach. 3. Prefunded wallets and stablecoins. Stripe’s Link balance is a prefunded wallet for agents, with Instinct as the first integration: fiat goes in through Stripe’s crypto onramp, becomes stablecoins on Tempo, sits in Privy non-custodial wallets, and gets spent through Stripe Issuing virtual debit cards. Mesh and Visa made crypto and stablecoin balances spendable at more than 175 million Visa merchant locations. Mastercard launched Agent Pay for Machines with Cloudflare on Base, where agents pay over x402. Now add the gatekeepers who can veto all three: Banks. Citi said it has “blocked anything that is trying to access our walls agentically,” except read-only open banking, while it builds a “know your agent” process. Reuters reported JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America also block external agents such as Muse, with Morgan Stanley and Schwab reported to do the same. Bank of America warned customers not to share banking credentials with AI assistants. Merchants. Per Benedict Evans, Amazon is blocking Muse and other consumer agents while Walmart supports them. StrictlyVC, citing The Verge, reported Amazon stripped product names from many order confirmation emails, apparently partly to keep AI firms from learning purchases through Gmail. Advertisers. Time.com ran ads that only AI agents can see, for Ally Bank and the Project Management Institute, built with ad tech startup Mobian. Time has since had more than 30 meetings with brands about similar ads, and some agent developers fear marketers could sway agents without users knowing. Agents do not just move purchases. They move balances. Mizuho cut its Circle target partly because AI assistants could steer USDC holders toward higher-yield, FDIC-insured options, and estimated USDC’s market cap could shrink by $4 billion to $9 billion. The truth: the credential is the moat Whoever issues the credential an agent spends with gets three things the agent maker does not: the identity, the purchase data and the liability. That is why the fight is over the card, not the chatbot. Diagram by the author Read the three architectures as bids for that position. Stripe’s virtual cards make Stripe the party that knows what the agent bought. Network tokens keep that knowledge with Visa, Mastercard and the issuing bank. Prefunded wallets move it to whoever holds the balance. Shopify adding network tokens to Shop Pay while Stripe pushes virtual cards and a Link balance for agents is two of the largest commerce platforms choosing different sides. The liability piece is the one nobody has solved. Axios, via Morning Brew, listed unclear liability for agent actions among the risks behind banks restricting access. Simon Taylor’s Personal Agent Protocol Map lays out the requirement: banks and merchants need verified identities, limited permissions and audit trails before they authorize agent actions, and access agreements could add fees that slow adoption. Citi’s “know your agent” is the first big bank saying out loud that agents will need their own KYC. If you are building an agent that touches money, here is what this week says to do: Never hold or replay a user’s bank login. Banks are blocking it, and Bank of America is telling customers not to allow it. Scope every spend. Approve the total in the conversation and issue a credential that only works for that purchase, the way Link does for Muse. Give the agent its own auditable identity. Know your agent is coming. Being ready for it is a distribution advantage. Assume the biggest merchants will block you. Partner with the ones that want agent traffic instead of scraping the ones that do not. Treat agent-only ads as untrusted input. If a page can carry ads only your agent sees, your agent needs a policy for them. My bet: network tokens win at the large merchants that already trust the networks, and scoped virtual cards and wallets win the long tail and machine to machine payments. Banks do not lose. They become the agent gatekeepers, which is the most valuable position of all. The line to remember The model decides what to buy. The credential decides who gets to know, and in payments, knowing is the business. Sources Figures and quotes are as reported by these outlets between Oct 26 and Oct 29, 2026, plus the pages linked below.
